hypotheses.label: conditional treatment probability
hypotheses.note: The probability of the event that treatment is assigned, computed under the law conditioned on the covariate cell {X = x}.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The propensity score, its balancing property and its role in adjustment are due to P. R. Rosenbaum and D. B. Rubin, "The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects," *Biometrika* **70** (1983), 41–55.

title: Complier Average Causal Effect
informal: For potential treatments $D(1),D(0)$ under a binary instrument, compliers are the units with $D(1)>D(0)$. The complier average causal effect is the conditional mean treatment effect among compliers: $$\tau_c=\mathbb E\!\left[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid D(1)>D(0)\right].$$
summary: The average causal effect of the instrument's assignment among units whose treatment it would change.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def cace (μ : Measure Ω) (d1 d0 : Ω → Bool) (y1 y0 : Ω → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ ω, (y1 ω - y0 ω) ∂(μ[|typeSet d1 d0 ComplianceType.complier])
formalizationNotes: Potential outcomes are indexed by the instrument, $Y(z)$, rather than by the pair (assignment, treatment received); this is the convention that lets the exclusion restriction be stated as $Y(1)=Y(0)$ on the units whose treatment the instrument does not change. If no unit is a complier the conditional measure is the zero measure and the definition returns 0; the identification theorems carry an explicit instrument-relevance hypothesis instead of relying on that value.

hypotheses.leanToken: ∫ ω, (y1 ω - y0 ω) ∂(μ[|typeSet d1 d0 ComplianceType.complier])
hypotheses.label: complier-conditional mean effect
hypotheses.note: The mean of Y(1) − Y(0) under the law conditioned on the event that the unit takes treatment when assigned to it and not otherwise.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The compliance-type taxonomy and this estimand are due to G. W. Imbens and J. D. Angrist, "Identification and estimation of local average treatment effects," *Econometrica* **62** (1994), 467–475, and J. D. Angrist, G. W. Imbens and D. B. Rubin, "Identification of causal effects using instrumental variables," *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **91** (1996), 444–455, in whose published discussion the competing names "local average treatment effect" and "complier average causal effect" were debated.

title: The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
informal: Fix an assignment vector $Z$ for a finite population and suppose at least one unit is left untreated, so that at least one potential outcome is never revealed. Then there exist two science tables that produce exactly the same observed outcome vector under $Z$ yet have different average causal effects.
summary: Two science tables can agree on every observed outcome under a fixed assignment yet have different average causal effects.
leanSignature:
theorem exists_sameObserved_ne_finiteATE (z : Assignment n)
    {i₀ : Fin n} (hi₀ : z i₀ = false) :
    ∃ S S' : ScienceTable n, S.observed z = S'.observed z ∧ S.finiteATE ≠ S'.finiteATE
formalizationNotes: The design-based form of the statement: the assignment is held fixed and the two witnesses differ only in potential outcomes that this assignment never reveals (both take the control column identically zero, and the second gives value 1 to the treated column of every untreated unit). The book states the obstruction in prose; the formal version makes it a non-identification theorem with explicit witnesses. The hypothesis that some unit is untreated is necessary — if every unit is treated the conclusion still holds for the symmetric reason, but the witnesses must be built from the control column instead.

hypotheses.label: an unrevealed outcome
hypotheses.note: Some unit is assigned to control, so its treated potential outcome is missing from the observed data.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The name and the sharp formulation are P. W. Holland's, "Statistics and causal inference," *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **81** (1986), 945–960; the missing-data reading of the science table that the argument exploits is developed throughout G. W. Imbens and D. B. Rubin, *Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences*, Cambridge University Press, 2015, Part I.

title: Completely Randomized Experiment
informal: A completely randomized experiment on $n$ units with $n_1$ treated draws the assignment vector uniformly from the set of all $0/1$ vectors with exactly $n_1$ ones, a set of size $\binom{n}{n_1}$; the hypothesis $n_1\le n$ is what makes that set nonempty.
summary: The uniform distribution on all assignment vectors with exactly n₁ treated units.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def completeDesign (n n₁ : ℕ) (h : n₁ ≤ n) : Design n :=
  ⟨completeSupport n n₁, completeSupport_nonempty h⟩
formalizationNotes: An assignment mechanism is modelled as a nonempty finite set of assignment vectors drawn uniformly, rather than as an arbitrary distribution on vectors; every design in the covered chapters (complete, stratified, matched-pair randomization) is of this form, and uniformity on the support is exactly what makes the randomization test exact. Bernoulli designs with success probability different from one half are outside this data type. The nonemptiness proof is packaged with the support, so a design always has at least one possible assignment.

hypotheses.label: fixed number treated
hypotheses.note: The support is the set of assignment vectors whose number of treated units is exactly n₁.

hypotheses.label: feasible allocation
hypotheses.note: At most n of the n units can be treated, which is what makes the support nonempty.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: Physical randomization as the basis of experimental inference is R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments*, Oliver & Boyd, Edinburgh, 1935; the repeated-sampling analysis of this particular mechanism goes back to J. Neyman, "On the application of probability theory to agricultural experiments. Essay on principles. Section 9" (1923), translated by D. M. Dabrowska and T. P. Speed, *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 465–472.

title: Neyman's Theorem: Unbiasedness of the Difference in Means
informal: Run a completely randomized experiment on $n$ units in which $n_1$ units are treated and $n_0$ are controls, with $n_1+n_0=n$, the assignment being drawn uniformly from all $\binom{n}{n_1}$ vectors with $n_1$ ones. Let $\hat\tau = \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0$ be the difference between the sample means of the observed outcomes in the two arms. Provided both arms are nonempty, the expectation of $\hat\tau$ over the randomization distribution is the finite-population average causal effect $\tau = n^{-1}\sum_i\{Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\}$.
summary: Under complete randomization the difference in sample means is unbiased for the finite-population average causal effect.
leanSignature:
theorem differenceInMeans_unbiased (S : ScienceTable n) (hsum : n₁ + n₀ = n)
    (h1 : 0 < n₁) (h0 : 0 < n₀) :
    (completeDesign n n₁ (by omega)).expect (diffInMeans S) = S.finiteATE
formalizationNotes: The proof goes through the affine representation of the difference in means on the support, where the arm sizes are constant, so that only the inclusion probability $\mathbb E[Z_i] = n_1/n$ is needed. Both arms are required to be nonempty because the arm sample mean divides by the realized arm size and would otherwise take the junk value 0; on the support of this design the realized sizes are exactly $n_1$ and $n_0$, so the hypothesis is the design condition of Ding's Definition 3.1 rather than an added restriction.

hypotheses.label: fixed arm sizes
hypotheses.note: The treated and control counts add up to the population size.

hypotheses.label: both arms nonempty
hypotheses.note: At least one unit is treated and at least one is a control, so both sample means are defined.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The repeated-sampling evaluation of the difference in means over the randomization distribution is J. Neyman, "On the application of probability theory to agricultural experiments. Essay on principles. Section 9" (1923), translated by D. M. Dabrowska and T. P. Speed, *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 465–472.

title: Neyman's Theorem: Exact Randomization Variance
informal: In a completely randomized experiment with $n_1$ treated and $n_0$ control units summing to $n$ and both arms nonempty, the variance of the difference in means $\hat\tau = \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0$ over the randomization distribution is exactly $$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\tau) \;=\; \frac{S^2(1)}{n_1}+\frac{S^2(0)}{n_0}-\frac{S^2(\tau)}{n},$$ where $S^2(1)$, $S^2(0)$ and $S^2(\tau)$ are the finite-population variances (divisor $n-1$) of the treated potential outcomes, of the control potential outcomes and of the individual effects, and the population has at least two units so that those divisors do not vanish.
summary: The randomization variance of the difference in means is the sum of the two arm variances minus the variance of the individual effects.
leanSignature:
theorem differenceInMeans_variance (S : ScienceTable n) (hsum : n₁ + n₀ = n)
    (h1 : 0 < n₁) (h0 : 0 < n₀)
    (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    (completeDesign n n₁ (by omega)).var (diffInMeans S)
      = popVar S.y1 / (n₁ : ℝ) + popVar S.y0 / (n₀ : ℝ) - popVar S.unitEffect / (n : ℝ)
formalizationNotes: The requirement of at least two units is added relative to the printed statement: the finite-population variances divide by $n-1$, and for a single unit Lean's division convention would make them the junk value 0. The proof computes the sampling-without-replacement variance of the affine form of $\hat\tau$ and then applies the identity $2S(1,0) = S^2(1)+S^2(0)-S^2(\tau)$ (Ding's Lemma 4.1), which is formalized separately, to convert the covariance term into the stated three-term shape.

hypotheses.label: fixed arm sizes
hypotheses.note: The treated and control counts add up to the population size.

hypotheses.label: both arms nonempty
hypotheses.note: At least one unit is treated and at least one is a control.

hypotheses.label: at least two units
hypotheses.note: The population has two or more units, so the finite-population variances with divisor n − 1 are defined.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The exact variance and the unidentifiability of its third term are J. Neyman, "On the application of probability theory to agricultural experiments. Essay on principles. Section 9" (1923), translated by D. M. Dabrowska and T. P. Speed, *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 465–472.

title: Exact Bias of Neyman's Variance Estimator
informal: Neyman's variance estimator for a completely randomized experiment is $\hat V = \hat s^2(1)/n_1 + \hat s^2(0)/n_0$, built from the two arm sample variances. With arm sizes summing to the population size, at least two units in each arm so that both sample variances are defined, and at least two units in the population, the expectation of $\hat V$ over the randomization distribution exceeds the true variance of the difference in means by exactly $$\mathbb E[\hat V]-\operatorname{Var}(\hat\tau) \;=\; \frac{S^2(\tau)}{n},$$ the finite-population variance of the individual effects divided by $n$.
summary: Neyman's variance estimator overestimates the true randomization variance by exactly the variance of the individual effects divided by n.
leanSignature:
theorem neymanVarEst_bias (S : ScienceTable n) (hsum : n₁ + n₀ = n)
    (h1 : 2 ≤ n₁) (h0 : 2 ≤ n₀)
    (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    (completeDesign n n₁ (by omega)).expect (neymanVarEst S)
        - (completeDesign n n₁ (by omega)).var (diffInMeans S)
      = popVar S.unitEffect / (n : ℝ)
formalizationNotes: The two-units-per-arm hypotheses are Ding's standing conditions for this part of Theorem 4.1: an arm sample variance divides by the realized arm size minus one. The requirement of at least two units in the population is added for the same reason as in the variance formula, so that the divisor n − 1 of the finite-population variances is nonzero. The identity is obtained by subtracting the exact randomization variance from the expectation of the estimator, both of which are proved separately.

hypotheses.label: fixed arm sizes
hypotheses.note: The treated and control counts add up to the population size.

hypotheses.label: two units per arm
hypotheses.note: Each arm contains at least two units, so its sample variance with divisor (arm size − 1) is defined.

hypotheses.label: at least two units
hypotheses.note: The population has two or more units, so the finite-population variance with divisor n − 1 is defined.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The estimator, its upward bias and the unidentifiability of the excess are already in J. Neyman, "On the application of probability theory to agricultural experiments. Essay on principles. Section 9" (1923), translated by D. M. Dabrowska and T. P. Speed, *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 465–472.

title: Conservativeness of Neyman's Variance Estimator
informal: In a completely randomized experiment with arm sizes summing to the population size, at least two units in each arm and at least two units overall, the expectation of Neyman's variance estimator $\hat V = \hat s^2(1)/n_1 + \hat s^2(0)/n_0$ is at least the true randomization variance of the difference in means.
summary: The expected value of Neyman's variance estimator is never below the true randomization variance.
leanSignature:
theorem neymanVarEst_conservative (S : ScienceTable n) (hsum : n₁ + n₀ = n)
    (h1 : 2 ≤ n₁) (h0 : 2 ≤ n₀) (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    (completeDesign n n₁ (by omega)).var (diffInMeans S)
      ≤ (completeDesign n n₁ (by omega)).expect (neymanVarEst S)
formalizationNotes: A direct consequence of the exact bias identity together with nonnegativity of a finite-population variance; the hypotheses are inherited from that identity. The statement is about the randomization distribution of the estimator, not about coverage of a particular interval — the normal approximation that turns conservativeness into conservative coverage is not part of this result.

hypotheses.label: fixed arm sizes
hypotheses.note: The treated and control counts add up to the population size.

hypotheses.label: two units per arm
hypotheses.note: Each arm contains at least two units, so its sample variance is defined.

hypotheses.label: at least two units
hypotheses.note: The population has two or more units, so the finite-population variances are defined.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: Conservativeness and its exactness under a constant effect are in J. Neyman, "On the application of probability theory to agricultural experiments. Essay on principles. Section 9" (1923), translated by D. M. Dabrowska and T. P. Speed, *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 465–472; the modern discussion of what the unidentifiable excess means for interval estimation is D. B. Rubin, "Comment: Neyman (1923) and causal inference in experiments and observational studies," *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 472–480.

title: Validity of the Fisher Randomization Test
informal: Let a design assign treatment by drawing an assignment vector uniformly from a nonempty finite set of possible vectors, and suppose Fisher's sharp null holds — every unit has $Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)$, so the treatment changes no unit's outcome. Take any statistic $T$ computed from a hypothetical assignment and the observed outcome vector, and define the randomization $p$-value at the realized assignment as the design probability that a re-randomized assignment gives a statistic value at least as large. Then for any level $\alpha \ge 0$, $$\Pr\bigl(p \le \alpha\bigr)\ \le\ \alpha,$$ so the test that rejects when $p\le\alpha$ has size at most $\alpha$.
summary: Under the sharp null the randomization p-value is super-uniform, so the randomization test has size at most alpha for any statistic.
leanSignature:
theorem sharpNull_prob_fisherPValue_le (D : Design n) (S : ScienceTable n)
    (hS : S.SharpNull)
    (T : Assignment n → (Fin n → ℝ) → ℝ) {α : ℝ}
    (hα : 0 ≤ α) :
    D.prob {z | fisherPValue D (fun z' => T z' (S.observed z')) z ≤ α} ≤ α
formalizationNotes: The nonnegative-level hypothesis is added: for a negative level the rejection event is empty and the inequality as stated would fail, so it delimits the statement rather than weakening it. Super-uniformity is proved combinatorially, by exhibiting a statistic-minimal rejected assignment that dominates the whole rejection event, and therefore needs no continuity or tie-breaking assumption; the possible atoms of the discrete randomization distribution are exactly why the bound is an inequality rather than an equality.

hypotheses.label: sharp null
hypotheses.note: Every unit has the same outcome under treatment and under control.

hypotheses.label: arbitrary test statistic
hypotheses.note: Any function of a hypothetical assignment and the observed outcome vector may be used.

hypotheses.label: nonnegative level
hypotheses.note: The nominal level is at least zero.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The randomization test is R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments*, Oliver & Boyd, Edinburgh, 1935, where it is introduced through the lady-tasting-tea experiment; the super-uniformity argument for discrete randomization distributions is standard, and is treated in E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer, 2022, in the chapters on permutation and randomization tests.

title: Unbiasedness of the Matched-Pair Estimator
informal: In a matched-pair experiment the $2m$ units are grouped into $m$ pairs matched on covariates, and within each pair an independent fair coin decides which of the two units is treated. Writing $D_j$ for the treated-minus-control difference of observed outcomes in pair $j$, the estimator is $\hat\tau = m^{-1}\sum_j D_j$. Its expectation over the uniform distribution on the $2^m$ coin-flip patterns is the average pair-level effect $\tau = m^{-1}\sum_j \tau_j$, where $\tau_j$ is the mean of the two units' individual effects in pair $j$.
summary: The average of the within-pair differences is unbiased for the average pair-level causal effect.
leanSignature:
theorem pairEstimator_unbiased (P : PairedTable m) :
    pairExpect P.pairEstimator = P.ate
formalizationNotes: A matched-pair assignment is exactly a choice, for each pair, of which member is treated, so the file models the design directly as the uniform law on Boolean vectors indexed by pairs rather than embedding it into a general assignment mechanism on $2m$ units. The coin-flip structure is then manifest and independence across pairs is by construction; the embedding adds nothing mathematically and is omitted. The estimand is the average of the pair-level effects, which equals the average of the $2m$ individual effects.

hypotheses.label: uniform coin flips
hypotheses.note: The expectation is taken over the uniform distribution on the 2^m patterns of within-pair coin flips.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: Blocking and pairing as devices for reducing experimental error go back to R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments*, Oliver & Boyd, Edinburgh, 1935; the design and its repeated-sampling analysis are treated at length in G. W. Imbens and D. B. Rubin, *Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences*, Cambridge University Press, 2015, ch. 10.

title: Bias of the Paired Variance Estimator
informal: In a matched-pair experiment with $m$ pairs and independent fair coins, let $D_j$ be the treated-minus-control difference in pair $j$, $\hat\tau = m^{-1}\sum_j D_j$ the estimator, and $\hat V = \{m(m-1)\}^{-1}\sum_j (D_j-\hat\tau)^2$ the usual variance estimator. Provided there are at least two pairs, so that $\hat V$ is defined, $$\mathbb E[\hat V]-\operatorname{Var}(\hat\tau)\;=\;\frac{1}{m(m-1)}\sum_{j}(\tau_j-\tau)^2,$$ where $\tau_j$ is the effect in pair $j$ and $\tau$ their average.
summary: The paired variance estimator exceeds the true variance by exactly the dispersion of the pair-level effects.
leanSignature:
theorem pairVarEst_bias (P : PairedTable m)
    (hm : 2 ≤ m) :
    pairExpect P.pairVarEst - pairVar P.pairEstimator
      = ((m : ℝ) * ((m : ℝ) - 1))⁻¹ * ∑ j, (P.pairEffect j - P.ate) ^ 2
formalizationNotes: The exact variance of the estimator, which the book leaves as an exercise, is proved first: pair differences from distinct pairs are uncorrelated because the coins are independent, so the variance is the average of the per-pair variances. The two-pair hypothesis is the condition under which the book's variance estimator is defined at all, its divisor being m(m − 1).

hypotheses.label: at least two pairs
hypotheses.note: There are two or more matched pairs, so the divisor m(m − 1) of the variance estimator is nonzero.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The conservativeness of the paired variance estimator and its exactness under a constant pair-level effect are of a piece with the completely randomized case of J. Neyman, "On the application of probability theory to agricultural experiments. Essay on principles. Section 9" (1923), translated by D. M. Dabrowska and T. P. Speed, *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 465–472, and are discussed in D. B. Rubin, "Comment: Neyman (1923) and causal inference in experiments and observational studies," *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 472–480.

title: Unbiasedness of the Stratified Estimator
informal: In a stratified randomized experiment the units are grouped by a discrete covariate into $K$ strata and an independent complete randomization is run inside each stratum, treating $m_k$ of the $n_{[k]}$ units of stratum $k$; the hypothesis $m_k \le n_{[k]}$ for every $k$ is what makes such an allocation possible. The stratified estimator is the size-weighted average of the within-stratum differences in means, $\hat\tau_S = \sum_k (n_{[k]}/n)\,\hat\tau_{[k]}$. If every stratum has units in both arms and the population is nonempty, then $\hat\tau_S$ is unbiased for the finite-population average causal effect.
summary: The size-weighted average of the within-stratum differences in means is unbiased for the population average causal effect.
leanSignature:
theorem stratifiedEstimator_unbiased (S : ScienceTable n) {g : Fin n → Fin K} {mk : Fin K → ℕ}
    (h : ∀ k, mk k ≤ (stratum g k).card)
    (h1 : ∀ k, 0 < mk k) (h0 : ∀ k, mk k < (stratum g k).card)
    (hn : 0 < n) :
    (stratifiedDesign g mk h).expect (stratifiedEstimator S g) = S.finiteATE
formalizationNotes: The proof deliberately avoids the product structure across strata. It uses only that the number of treated units in a stratum is constant on the support, and that the design is invariant under transpositions of two units within a stratum, which forces the inclusion probability to be $m_k/n_{[k]}$ for every unit of stratum $k$. The nonempty-population hypothesis is added so that the factor $n^{-1}$ in the estimand is not a junk value. The exact stratified variance is not formalized: it requires the full independence-across-strata factorization, and the book itself obtains it by applying the completely randomized variance formula stratum by stratum.

hypotheses.label: feasible allocation
hypotheses.note: In each stratum the number of units to be treated does not exceed the stratum size.

hypotheses.leanToken: (h1 : ∀ k, 0 < mk k) (h0 : ∀ k, mk k < (stratum g k).card)
hypotheses.label: both arms in every stratum
hypotheses.note: Every stratum has at least one treated and at least one control unit, so its difference in means is defined.

hypotheses.label: nonempty population
hypotheses.note: There is at least one unit, so the stratum weights sum to one.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: Stratification (blocking) as a device of experimental design is R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments*, Oliver & Boyd, Edinburgh, 1935; the modern treatment of stratified randomized experiments is G. W. Imbens and D. B. Rubin, *Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences*, Cambridge University Press, 2015, ch. 9.

title: The Regression Coefficient of Treatment is the Difference in Means
informal: Regress the observed outcome on an intercept and the treatment indicator. If the pair $(a,b)$ solves the two least-squares normal equations — the residuals sum to zero and are orthogonal to the treatment indicator — and both arms are nonempty, then the slope is exactly the difference in means, $b = \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0$, and the intercept is the control arm mean.
summary: The least-squares coefficient of a binary treatment indicator equals the difference in sample means.
leanSignature:
theorem olsCoeff_eq_diffInMeans (S : ScienceTable n) {z : Assignment n} {a b : ℝ}
    (hfit : IsOLSFit S z a b)
    (h1 : 0 < (armIdx z true).card) (h0 : 0 < (armIdx z false).card) :
    b = diffInMeans S z
formalizationNotes: Stated as "any solution of the normal equations has this slope" rather than as a statement about a minimizer, which avoids an existence-and-uniqueness claim and matches the form the book uses. The two normal equations are solved directly for a binary regressor rather than through a general least-squares interface. Both arms must be nonempty: otherwise the regressor is constant, the design matrix drops rank and the slope is not identified. Lin's estimator, the coefficient of treatment in the fully interacted regression, is not formalized.

hypotheses.label: normal equations
hypotheses.note: The residuals of the fit sum to zero and are orthogonal to the treatment indicator.

hypotheses.label: both arms nonempty
hypotheses.note: The realized assignment treats at least one unit and leaves at least one untreated, so the regressor is not constant.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The cautionary analysis of regression adjustment in randomized experiments is D. A. Freedman, "On regression adjustments to experimental data," *Advances in Applied Mathematics* **40** (2008), 180–193; the repair, showing that the fully interacted adjustment cannot hurt asymptotically, is W. Lin, "Agnostic notes on regression adjustments to experimental data: reexamining Freedman's critique," *Annals of Applied Statistics* **7** (2013), 295–318.

title: Unbiasedness of Covariate Adjustment with Fixed Coefficients
informal: Given a covariate vector $x$ measured before assignment and fixed numbers $\beta_1,\beta_0$, the covariate-adjusted estimator is $$\hat\tau(\beta_1,\beta_0)\;=\;\bigl(\bar Y_1-\beta_1(\bar x_1-\bar x)\bigr)-\bigl(\bar Y_0-\beta_0(\bar x_0-\bar x)\bigr),$$ each arm mean being corrected for the chance imbalance of the covariate in that arm. Under complete randomization with arm sizes summing to the population size and both arms nonempty, this estimator is unbiased for the finite-population average causal effect, for every choice of the coefficients.
summary: For any fixed adjustment coefficients, the covariate-adjusted estimator remains unbiased under complete randomization.
leanSignature:
theorem adjEstimator_unbiased (S : ScienceTable n) (x : Fin n → ℝ) (β1 β0 : ℝ)
    (hsum : n₁ + n₀ = n)
    (h1 : 0 < n₁) (h0 : 0 < n₀) :
    (completeDesign n n₁ (by omega)).expect (adjEstimator S x β1 β0) = S.finiteATE
formalizationNotes: The coefficients are fixed constants, not estimated from the realized data; with estimated coefficients the estimator is no longer exactly unbiased and the relevant statement is asymptotic. That asymptotic theory, and the efficiency comparison between the unadjusted and the fully interacted adjusted estimator, are outside the scope of this file. Taking both coefficients zero recovers the difference in means.

hypotheses.label: fixed arm sizes
hypotheses.note: The treated and control counts add up to the population size.

hypotheses.label: both arms nonempty
hypotheses.note: At least one unit is treated and at least one is a control.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: That adjustment with estimated coefficients can degrade the estimator in finite samples is D. A. Freedman, "On regression adjustments to experimental data," *Advances in Applied Mathematics* **40** (2008), 180–193; that the fully interacted version cannot hurt asymptotically is W. Lin, "Agnostic notes on regression adjustments to experimental data: reexamining Freedman's critique," *Annals of Applied Statistics* **7** (2013), 295–318.

title: Selection-Bias Decomposition of the Prima Facie Effect
informal: The prima facie effect is the naive comparison of observed outcomes across arms, $\tau_{\mathrm{PF}} = \mathbb E[Y\mid Z=1]-\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=0]$. With a measurable treatment indicator and integrable potential outcomes, it decomposes exactly as $$\tau_{\mathrm{PF}} \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid Z=1]}_{\text{effect on the treated}}\;+\;\underbrace{\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid Z=1]-\mathbb E[Y(0)\mid Z=0]}_{\text{selection bias}}.$$
summary: The naive between-arm contrast equals the effect on the treated plus a selection-bias term comparing the arms on the control potential outcome.
leanSignature:
theorem primaFacie_eq_att_add_selectionBias [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (hZ : Measurable Z)
    (hi1 : Integrable y1 μ) (hi0 : Integrable y0 μ) :
    primaFacie μ Z (obs Z y1 y0)
      = att μ Z y1 y0
        + (∫ ω, y0 ω ∂(μ[|treatedEvent Z]) - ∫ ω, y0 ω ∂(μ[|{ω | Z ω = false}]))
formalizationNotes: The decomposition is an algebraic identity of conditional integrals once consistency — that on the treated arm the observed outcome is the treated potential outcome — is available, and that step needs the conditioning event to be measurable, which is what the measurability hypothesis supplies. Integrability is required for the conditional mean of a difference to split. The book presents the decomposition as an unnumbered display in the text.

title: Identification by Standardization (the g-Formula)
informal: Let the covariate $X$ take finitely many values and write $m_z(x) = \mathbb E[Y\mid Z=z, X=x]$ for the arm regression functions — quantities computable from the observed data. Assume unconfoundedness: within every covariate cell the pair of potential outcomes is independent of treatment and overlap: every covariate cell that carries mass has treatment probability strictly between $0$ and $1$, together with measurability of the model variables and integrable potential outcomes. Then the average causal effect is identified by the covariate-weighted contrast of the two regression functions, $$\tau\;=\;\sum_x \Pr(X=x)\,\bigl\{m_1(x)-m_0(x)\bigr\}.$$
summary: Under unconfoundedness and overlap, the average causal effect is the covariate-weighted contrast of the two arm regression functions.

    (hi1 : Integrable y1 μ) (hi0 : Integrable y0 μ) :

      = ∑ x : 𝒳, (μ (cell X x)).toReal

formalizationNotes: Stated for a covariate with finitely many values, so the identification formula is a finite sum over covariate cells and conditioning is on events of positive probability; the general-covariate version replaces the sum by an integral against the law of X and the cell means by conditional expectations, with no change in statistical content. Cells of probability zero contribute zero to both sides and need no hypothesis. The theorem is proved under full cell-wise independence rather than the weaker equality of arm-conditional means that the book's hypotheses state; the mean-ignorability version is recorded separately in the same file.

title: Identification by Inverse-Probability Weighting
informal: Weight every treated unit by the reciprocal of its propensity score $e(X)=\Pr(Z=1\mid X)$ and every control unit by the reciprocal of $1-e(X)$. Under unconfoundedness, overlap, measurability of the model variables and integrable potential outcomes, the weighted contrast of observed outcomes identifies the average causal effect: $$\tau\;=\;\mathbb E\Bigl[\frac{ZY}{e(X)}-\frac{(1-Z)Y}{1-e(X)}\Bigr].$$
summary: Reweighting the observed arms by the inverse propensity score identifies the average causal effect.

title: The Product-Bias Identity for the Augmented Functional
informal: Given a working propensity model $\bar e$ and a working outcome model $\bar m_1$, both arbitrary functions of the covariate, the augmented inverse-probability-weighting functional for the treated mean is $$\tilde\mu_1 \;=\; \mathbb E\Bigl[\bar m_1(X)+\frac{Z\{Y-\bar m_1(X)\}}{\bar e(X)}\Bigr].$$ Under unconfoundedness, overlap for the true propensity score, measurability of the model variables, an integrable treated potential outcome and a working propensity that never vanishes, the error of this functional is exactly $$\tilde\mu_1-\mathbb E[Y(1)]\;=\;\sum_x \Pr(X=x)\,\frac{e(x)-\bar e(x)}{\bar e(x)}\bigl\{m_1(x)-\bar m_1(x)\bigr\},$$ a sum of products of the two model errors.
summary: The error of the augmented treated functional is a covariate-weighted sum of products of the propensity-model error and the outcome-model error.
leanSignature:
theorem aipwTreated_sub_integral_y1_eq [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (hu : Unconfounded μ Z y1 y0 X)
    (hpos : Positive μ Z X)
    (hy1 : Measurable y1) (hy0 : Measurable y0) (hZ : Measurable Z) (hX : Measurable X)
    (hi1 : Integrable y1 μ)
    (hebar : ∀ x, ebar x ≠ 0) :
    aipwTreated μ Z X (obs Z y1 y0) ebar m1bar - ∫ ω, y1 ω ∂μ
      = ∑ x : 𝒳, (μ (cell X x)).toReal
          * ((propensity μ Z X x - ebar x) / ebar x
              * (cellMean μ Z X (obs Z y1 y0) true x - m1bar x))
formalizationNotes: The working models are arbitrary user-supplied functions of the covariate, not required to be correct — that is the whole point of the construction. The hypothesis that the working propensity never vanishes is a condition on the working model, separate from the overlap condition on the true propensity score; without it the functional is not even defined. In the book this identity appears inside the proof of the double-robustness theorem and again in the discussion of the estimator, and carries no number of its own. This is the algebraic double robustness of the population functional; asymptotic normality, efficiency and cross-fitting for the sample version are out of scope.

title: Double Robustness: Correct Propensity Model
informal: The doubly robust functional for the average causal effect combines a working propensity model $\bar e$ with working outcome models $\bar m_1, \bar m_0$, $$\tilde\tau \;=\; \mathbb E\Bigl[\bar m_1(X)+\frac{Z\{Y-\bar m_1(X)\}}{\bar e(X)}\Bigr]-\mathbb E\Bigl[\bar m_0(X)+\frac{(1-Z)\{Y-\bar m_0(X)\}}{1-\bar e(X)}\Bigr].$$ Assume unconfoundedness, overlap for the true propensity score, measurability of the model variables and integrable potential outcomes. If the working propensity model is the true propensity score and the working weights are finite, that is $\bar e$ is never $0$ or $1$, then $\tilde\tau = \tau$ — whatever the outcome models are.
summary: If the working propensity model is correct, the augmented functional identifies the average causal effect whatever the outcome models.

title: Identification of the Effect on the Treated by Outcome Regression
informal: The average causal effect on the treated, $\tau_T = \mathbb E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid Z=1]$, needs less than $\tau$ does: the treated units' own treated outcomes are observed, so only the control potential outcome has to be ignorable and only one-sided overlap is required. Assume the control potential outcome is ignorable given the covariate and every covariate cell that carries mass contains control units, together with measurability of the model variables, integrable potential outcomes and a treated arm of positive probability. Then $$\tau_T\;=\;\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=1]\;-\;\sum_x \Pr(X=x\mid Z=1)\,m_0(x),$$ where $m_0(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=0,X=x]$ is the control regression function: the treated units' observed mean, minus what those same units would have averaged had they been untreated, imputed cell by cell from the controls.
summary: Under one-sided ignorability and overlap, the effect on the treated is the treated mean minus the treated-weighted average of the control regression function.

The covariate weights on the right are those of the treated subpopulation, which are obtained from the marginal weights by tilting with the propensity odds. The requirement that some unit be treated is what makes the conditional law on the treated arm a probability measure rather than the zero measure.

title: The Propensity Tilt Gives the Effect on the Treated
informal: For a weight function $h$ of the covariate, the $h$-weighted average treatment effect is $$\tau_h\;=\;\frac{\mathbb E[h(X)\{Y(1)-Y(0)\}]}{\mathbb E[h(X)]},$$ the average causal effect computed after tilting the covariate distribution by $h$; taking $h\equiv 1$ recovers $\tau$, and $h = e(1-e)$ gives the overlap-weighted effect. Taking $h$ to be the propensity score itself reproduces the treated subpopulation: assuming unconfoundedness, measurability of the model variables, integrable potential outcomes and a treated arm of positive probability, one has $\tau_e = \tau_T$.
summary: Tilting the covariate distribution by the propensity score turns the weighted average effect into the effect on the treated.

title: Adjusting for the Propensity Score Suffices
informal: Assume unconfoundedness given the covariate, overlap, measurability of the model variables and an integrable treated potential outcome. Fix a value $v$ of the propensity score with a level set of positive probability and $v>0$. Then inside that level set the treated arm's mean of the treated potential outcome equals its overall mean there, $$\mathbb E\bigl[Y(1)\mid Z=1,\ e(X)=v\bigr]\;=\;\mathbb E\bigl[Y(1)\mid e(X)=v\bigr].$$
summary: Unconfoundedness given the covariate implies unconfoundedness given the propensity score, in mean form.
leanSignature:
theorem integral_cond_propensityLevel_arm_eq [IsProbabilityMeasure μ]
    (hu : Unconfounded μ Z y1 y0 X)
    (hpos : Positive μ Z X)
    (hy1 : Measurable y1) (hy0 : Measurable y0) (hZ : Measurable Z) (hX : Measurable X)
    (hint : Integrable y1 μ) {v : ℝ}
    (hlevel : μ (propensityLevel μ Z X v) ≠ 0)
    (hv : 0 < v) :
    ∫ ω, y1 ω ∂(μ[|treatedEvent Z ∩ propensityLevel μ Z X v])
      = ∫ ω, y1 ω ∂(μ[|propensityLevel μ Z X v])
formalizationNotes: The book states the conclusion as a conditional independence of the potential outcomes and the treatment given the propensity score. What is proved here is its mean form: within a level set of the propensity score the arm-conditional mean of a potential outcome equals its unconditional mean. That is the form every downstream identification result consumes, and it avoids constructing a conditional-independence-given-a-real-valued-statistic layer. The positivity of the level is what lets the common factor cancel between numerator and denominator when passing to the treated part.

title: Subclassification on the Propensity Score Identifies the Average Causal Effect
informal: Split the population into subclasses, take the difference of the two arm means inside each subclass, and average the results with the subclass probabilities as weights. Assume unconfoundedness, overlap, measurability of the model variables and integrable potential outcomes. If the subclasses are exactly the level sets of the propensity score — two covariate values share a subclass precisely when they share a propensity value, then this subclassification estimand equals the average causal effect.
summary: Stratifying on the level sets of the propensity score and averaging the within-stratum contrasts identifies the average causal effect.

    [Fintype 𝒦] (hu : Unconfounded μ Z y1 y0 X) (hpos : Positive μ Z X)
    (hy1 : Measurable y1) (hy0 : Measurable y0) (hZ : Measurable Z) (hX : Measurable X)

title: The Matching Bias is Controlled by the Match Quality
informal: Matching imputes a treated unit's missing control outcome from a matched control. When the match is not exact the imputation carries a bias equal to the discrepancy of the control regression function between the unit's covariate value and its match's, $m_0(X_i) - m_0(X_{j(i)})$. If the control regression function is Lipschitz in the covariate with constant $L$, where $L$ is nonnegative, this bias is at most $L$ times the distance between a unit and its match, $$\bigl|m_0(X_i)-m_0(X_{j(i)})\bigr|\ \le\ L\,d\bigl(X_i, X_{j(i)}\bigr).$$
summary: If the control regression function is Lipschitz, the bias of an inexact match is at most the Lipschitz constant times the covariate distance to the match.
leanSignature:
theorem abs_matchingBias_le [PseudoMetricSpace 𝒳] {j : Ω → Ω} {L : ℝ} {Y : Ω → ℝ}
    (hL : LipschitzWith (Real.toNNReal L) (cellMean μ Z X Y false))
    (hL0 : 0 ≤ L) (ω : Ω) :
    |matchingBias μ Z X Y j ω| ≤ L * dist (X ω) (X (j ω))
formalizationNotes: The covariate is given a pseudometric so that "match quality" has a meaning; the bound itself is a pointwise deterministic estimate with no probabilistic content, the probabilistic input being confined to the definition of the control regression function. The nonnegativity of the constant is added so that the real number L agrees with the nonnegative constant carried by the Lipschitz predicate. What is formalized is the population, estimand-level statement; the finite-sample matching estimator with several nearest neighbours, its bias-corrected version and their asymptotics are out of scope.

title: Trimming Changes the Estimand
informal: Limited overlap is the practical failure mode of weighting: as the propensity score approaches $0$ or $1$ the inverse-probability weights explode. Trimming discards the units whose propensity score falls outside a band $[\eta, 1-\eta]$, which restores stability but changes what is being estimated. With measurable treatment and covariate, an integrable individual effect and a retained population of positive probability, the trimmed estimand is $$\mathbb E\bigl[Y(1)-Y(0)\ \big|\ \eta \le e(X) \le 1-\eta\bigr] \;=\; \frac{\sum_{x:\, \eta \le e(x) \le 1-\eta} \Pr(X=x)\,\tau(x)}{\Pr\bigl(\eta\le e(X)\le 1-\eta\bigr)},$$ the covariate-weighted average of the conditional effects over the retained cells only.
summary: The trimmed analysis identifies the average causal effect over the retained subpopulation, not the population effect.
leanSignature:
theorem trimmedATE_eq_sum_cate [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] [DecidableEq 𝒳] {η : ℝ}
    (hZ : Measurable Z) (hX : Measurable X)
    (hint : Integrable (fun ω => y1 ω - y0 ω) μ)
    (hne : μ (trimmedSet μ Z X η) ≠ 0) :
    trimmedATE μ Z X y1 y0 η
      = (∑ x ∈ Finset.univ.filter fun x =>
            η ≤ propensity μ Z X x ∧ propensity μ Z X x ≤ 1 - η,
          (μ (cell X x)).toReal * cate μ X y1 y0 x)
        / (μ (trimmedSet μ Z X η)).toReal
formalizationNotes: That trimming changes the estimand is prose in the reference, discussed with pointers to the literature rather than proved as a numbered theorem; the statement formalized here is the precise version of that warning. The retained population is the union of the covariate cells whose propensity score lies in the band, so conditioning on it is elementary conditioning on a positive-probability event — which is what the last hypothesis provides. A companion result in the same file shows the trimmed estimand coincides with the average causal effect exactly under a homogeneous conditional effect. The book's quantitative covariate-imbalance bound under strict overlap is not formalized, as it depends on distributional constants the book imports rather than develops.

title: The First Stage is the Complier Proportion
informal: With a binary instrument $Z$, potential treatments $D(1), D(0)$ and observed treatment $D = D(Z)$, assume random assignment: the instrument is independent of the potential treatments and potential outcomes and monotonicity: no unit is a defier, so $D(1)\ge D(0)$, together with measurability of the model variables and both instrument arms of positive probability. Then the first-stage contrast is exactly the proportion of compliers, $$\mathbb E[D\mid Z=1]-\mathbb E[D\mid Z=0]\;=\;\Pr\bigl(D(1)>D(0)\bigr).$$
summary: Under random assignment and monotonicity the first-stage contrast equals the proportion of compliers.

formalizationNotes: Random assignment is stated as independence of the instrument from the whole quadruple of potential treatments and potential outcomes, which is the book's assumption; the potential outcomes appear in the hypothesis even though the conclusion mentions only the treatment, because the same independence predicate is reused across the file. Monotonicity is stated pointwise, unit by unit, as in the book, rather than in distribution. The compliance-type events are measurable because they are preimages under the pair of potential treatments.

title: The LATE Theorem: the Ratio of Reduced Form to First Stage
informal: Assume the three instrumental-variable conditions: random assignment of the instrument, monotonicity — no defiers and the exclusion restriction — units whose treatment the instrument does not change have equal potential outcomes, together with measurability of the model variables, integrable potential outcomes, both instrument arms of positive probability and instrument relevance: the first-stage contrast is nonzero. title: Instrumental Inequality
informal: For a binary outcome, the instrumental-variable assumptions are not vacuous — they constrain the observed distribution. Under random assignment of the instrument, monotonicity and the exclusion restriction, with measurability of the model variables and both instrument arms of positive probability, the contrast of the observable product $DY$ across instrument arms is nonnegative: $$\mathbb E[DY\mid Z=1]-\mathbb E[DY\mid Z=0]\ \ge\ 0.$$

    (hviol : ittContrast μ Z
        (fun ω => ind (obsTreat Z d1 d0 ω) * ind (obsBool Z b1 b0 ω)) < 0) :
    ¬ (IVRandomized μ Z d1 d0 (fun ω => ind (b1 ω)) (fun ω => ind (b0 ω))
        ∧ NoDefiers d1 d0
        ∧ ExclusionRestriction d1 d0 (fun ω => ind (b1 ω)) (fun ω => ind (b0 ω)))
formalizationNotes: Stated as the contrapositive of the first instrumental inequality; the other three inequalities give analogous refutations and are not separately stated in this form. What is refuted is the conjunction of the three assumptions, not any one of them: a violation says the package is untenable but does not say which component fails. The observable contrast is expressed through the potential quantities that generate it, which is how the statement can be about a distribution while the hypothesis is checkable from the observed data.

(hZ : Measurable Z) (hd1 : Measurable d1) (hd0 : Measurable d0)
    (hb1 : Measurable b1) (hb0 : Measurable b0)
hypotheses.label: measurability
hypotheses.note: The instrument, the potential treatments and the binary potential outcomes are measurable.

hypotheses.leanToken: (hZ1 : μ {ω | Z ω = true} ≠ 0) (hZ0 : μ {ω | Z ω = false} ≠ 0)
hypotheses.label: both instrument arms nonnull
hypotheses.note: Both values of the instrument occur with positive probability, so the two arm means are defined.

(hviol : ittContrast μ Z
        (fun ω => ind (obsTreat Z d1 d0 ω) * ind (obsBool Z b1 b0 ω)) < 0)
hypotheses.label: observed violation
hypotheses.note: The across-arm contrast of the product of received treatment and outcome is strictly negative.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: That the instrumental-variable model has observable consequences, and what they are, is A. Balke and J. Pearl, "Bounds on treatment effects from studies with imperfect compliance," *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **92** (1997), 1171–1176, following J. Pearl, "On the testability of causal models with latent and instrumental variables," in *Proceedings of the Eleventh Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence*, Morgan Kaufmann, 1995, pp. 435–443.

title: Manski Worst-Case Bounds on the Average Causal Effect
informal: Without any identification assumption the average causal effect is not identified, but it is not arbitrary either. Suppose the treatment indicator is measurable, both potential outcomes are integrable and both potential outcomes take values in a known range $[\ell, u]$. Writing $p=\Pr(Z=1)$ and filling each missing potential outcome in with its extreme values gives $$p\,\mathbb E[Y\mid Z{=}1]+(1-p)\ell-p\,u-(1-p)\mathbb E[Y\mid Z{=}0]\ \le\ \tau\ \le\ p\,\mathbb E[Y\mid Z{=}1]+(1-p)u-p\,\ell-(1-p)\mathbb E[Y\mid Z{=}0].$$
summary: With outcomes known to lie in a fixed range, the average causal effect lies in an explicit interval computable from the observed data.
leanSignature:
theorem ate_mem_manski_Icc [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hZ : Measurable Z)
    (hi1 : Integrable y1 μ) (hi0 : Integrable y0 μ)
    (hb1 : ∀ ω, y1 ω ∈ Set.Icc lo hi) (hb0 : ∀ ω, y0 ω ∈ Set.Icc lo hi) :
    ate μ y1 y0 ∈ Set.Icc (manskiLowerATE μ Z (obs Z y1 y0) lo hi)
      (manskiUpperATE μ Z (obs Z y1 y0) lo hi)
formalizationNotes: The whole argument rests on the two-arm split of a mean potential outcome, in which only the unobserved summand needs bounding. The book derives the bounds as unnumbered displays. Sharpness — that both endpoints are attained by genuine potential-outcome laws with the same observed-data distribution — is not stated in the reference but is proved in the same file, by exhibiting potential outcomes that agree with the given ones on the observed arm and take the extreme value on the unobserved arm.

hypotheses.label: measurable treatment
hypotheses.note: The treatment indicator is a random variable, so the two arms are measurable events.

hypotheses.leanToken: (hi1 : Integrable y1 μ) (hi0 : Integrable y0 μ)
hypotheses.label: integrable outcomes
hypotheses.note: Both potential outcomes have finite mean.

hypotheses.leanToken: (hb1 : ∀ ω, y1 ω ∈ Set.Icc lo hi) (hb0 : ∀ ω, y0 ω ∈ Set.Icc lo hi)
hypotheses.label: known outcome range
hypotheses.note: Every unit's two potential outcomes lie in the interval from the known lower to the known upper limit.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The bounds are C. F. Manski, "Nonparametric bounds on treatment effects," *American Economic Review* **80** (1990), 319–323; the general programme of reporting what the data identify without untestable assumptions is developed in C. F. Manski, *Partial Identification of Probability Distributions*, Springer, New York, 2003.

title: The Manski Interval has Width Exactly the Outcome Range
informal: With a measurable treatment indicator and any observed outcome variable, the difference between the upper and lower worst-case bounds on the average causal effect is exactly $u-\ell$, the a priori range of the outcome — whatever the data, whatever the treated fraction.
summary: The upper and lower worst-case bounds differ by exactly the width of the outcome range, whatever the data.
leanSignature:
theorem manski_width [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] (hZ : Measurable Z) (Y : Ω → ℝ) :
    manskiUpperATE μ Z Y lo hi - manskiLowerATE μ Z Y lo hi = hi - lo
formalizationNotes: A cancellation: the identified parts of the two endpoints are the same, and what survives is the treated fraction times the outcome range plus the control fraction times the same range. The statement is about the two bound functionals themselves, so it needs no assumption on the outcome variable — not even that it is the observed outcome of a potential-outcome pair, nor that it lies in the stated range.

hypotheses.label: measurable treatment
hypotheses.note: The treatment indicator is a random variable, so the two arm probabilities sum to one.

hypotheses.label: arbitrary outcome variable
hypotheses.note: The identity holds for any real-valued outcome variable, with no range or integrability restriction.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The observation that the assumption-free bound has width equal to the outcome range, so that it can never be a point identification, is C. F. Manski, "Nonparametric bounds on treatment effects," *American Economic Review* **80** (1990), 319–323; see also C. F. Manski, *Partial Identification of Probability Distributions*, Springer, New York, 2003.

title: Rosenbaum's Worst Case is the Extreme Tilt
informal: In a matched observational study the assignment within a pair is not a fair coin: hidden confounding can tilt it. Rosenbaum's sensitivity model bounds the tilt by one parameter, requiring each pair's treatment probability to lie in the band $[1/(1+\Gamma), \Gamma/(1+\Gamma)]$ for a sensitivity parameter $\Gamma\ge1$. For a sign-score statistic $T=\sum_j S_jq_j$ with nonnegative scores $q_j$ — the family that contains the sign test, the paired $t$ statistic and Wilcoxon's signed-rank statistic — the upper-tail probability of $T$ under any law in the model is at most its value under the extreme tilt in which every pair has probability $\Gamma/(1+\Gamma)$.
summary: The tail probability of a nonnegative sign-score statistic under Rosenbaum's model is largest at the extreme assignment tilt.
leanSignature:
theorem biasedTail_le_extreme {π : Fin m → ℝ} {q : Fin m → ℝ} {t Γ : ℝ}
    (hq : ∀ i, 0 ≤ q i)
    (hmodel : RosenbaumModel π Γ)
    (hΓ : 1 ≤ Γ) :
    biasedTail π q t ≤ biasedTail (fun _ => Γ / (1 + Γ)) q t
formalizationNotes: This is the exact finite-sample core of the book's §19.2 — the stochastic-dominance statement that makes the worst case worst. The normal approximation to the resulting $p$-value, which the book passes to immediately afterwards, is not formalized: it would require a Lindeberg-type central limit theorem for weighted Bernoulli sums, and it is an approximation rather than an identity. The dominance is proved by a one-coordinate-at-a-time exchange argument: raising a single pair's probability can only increase the tail, because conditionally on the other coordinates the statistic is monotone in that pair's sign. A companion result shows the bound degrades monotonically in the sensitivity parameter, and that the parameter value one is exactly the randomized case of fair coins.

hypotheses.label: nonnegative scores
hypotheses.note: Every pair's score in the sign-score statistic is nonnegative.

hypotheses.label: bounded hidden bias
hypotheses.note: Each pair's treatment probability lies within the odds-ratio band determined by the sensitivity parameter.

hypotheses.label: genuine sensitivity parameter
hypotheses.note: The sensitivity parameter is at least one, the value corresponding to no hidden bias.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The sensitivity model, the sign-score family and the worst-case argument are P. R. Rosenbaum, *Observational Studies*, 2nd ed., Springer, New York, 2002, ch. 4, where the odds-ratio parameter is introduced and the design sensitivity of the resulting procedures is analysed.

title: The E-Value is a Valid Threshold for Unmeasured Confounding
informal: Cornfield's inequality bounds an observed risk ratio by the bounding factor of the two confounding associations, $\beta(w_1,w_2)=w_1w_2/(w_1+w_2-1)$, where $w_1$ measures the association between the treatment and an unmeasured binary confounder and $w_2$ that between the confounder and the outcome. Let the observed risk ratio be at least one and both confounding associations be at least one. If the confounding is strong enough to explain the observed association away, that is the observed risk ratio does not exceed the bounding factor, then $$\max(w_1,w_2)\ \ge\ E \;=\; \mathrm{RR}+\sqrt{\mathrm{RR}(\mathrm{RR}-1)}.$$
summary: Explaining away an observed risk ratio requires at least one confounding association of size the E-value.
leanSignature:
theorem lt_of_boundingFactor_ge {rr w₁ w₂ : ℝ} (hrr : 1 ≤ rr) (h₁ : 1 ≤ w₁) (h₂ : 1 ≤ w₂)
    (hexplain : rr ≤ boundingFactor w₁ w₂) :
    eValue rr ≤ max w₁ w₂
formalizationNotes: What is formalized is the algebra of the bound: the properties of the bounding factor, the reduction of the two-parameter problem to the larger association, and the threshold characterization. The probabilistic derivation of Cornfield's inequality from a latent-ignorability model is not formalized in this release; the inequality is taken as the starting point, and what is proved is exactly the part a practitioner uses. That the threshold is attained — so the E-value is the least such number, not merely some such number — is proved separately in the same file, by taking both associations equal to the E-value.

hypotheses.label: risk ratio at least one
hypotheses.note: The observed risk ratio is at least one, the orientation in which the E-value is defined.

hypotheses.label: confounding associations at least one
hypotheses.note: Both confounding risk ratios are at least one.

hypotheses.label: association explained away
hypotheses.note: The observed risk ratio does not exceed what confounding of the given strengths could produce.

reference.formal: P. Ding, *A First Course in Causal Inference*, Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, 2024 (arXiv:2305.18793).
reference.biblio: The bounding argument originates with J. Cornfield, W. Haenszel, E. C. Hammond, A. M. Lilienfeld, M. B. Shimkin and E. L. Wynder, "Smoking and lung cancer: recent evidence and a discussion of some questions," *Journal of the National Cancer Institute* **22** (1959), 173–203; its sharpness is P. Ding and T. J. VanderWeele, "Sensitivity analysis without assumptions," *Epidemiology* **27** (2016), 368–377, and the inverted one-number summary is T. J. VanderWeele and P. Ding, "Sensitivity analysis in observational research: introducing the E-value," *Annals of Internal Medicine* **167** (2017), 268–274.

title: Finite-Population Summaries
informal: For a finite population of $N$ units with values $y_i$, the finite-population variance is $$S_y^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i (y_i-\bar y)^2,\qquad \bar y=\frac1N\sum_i y_i.$$
summary: The total, mean and (N-1)-normalised variance of a deterministic quantity on a fixed finite population, together with their elementary algebra.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def populationVariance (y : U → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ((Fintype.card U : ℝ) - 1)⁻¹ * ∑ i, (y i - populationMean y) ^ 2
formalizationNotes: Degenerate populations are handled by Lean's `(0 : ℝ)⁻¹ = 0` convention rather than by side conditions: the mean of an empty population is $0$, and the variance is $0$ whenever $N \le 1$. Statements whose mathematical content would be lost under that convention carry explicit cardinality hypotheses instead — the characterisation of vanishing variance as constancy of $y$ is stated for $N \ge 2$, and the centred-values-sum-to-zero identity assumes the population nonempty. The fixed-units, fixed-values convention is Mead's finite model (§9.4–§9.5); the $N-1$ normalisation is the survey-sampling one.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The fixed-population view of experimental data, in which the unit values are constants and the only randomness is the allocation, goes back to J. Neyman, “On the application of probability theory to agricultural experiments. Essay on principles. Section 9” (1923), translated by D. M. Dabrowska and T. P. Speed in *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 465–472. The $N-1$ normalisation of $S_y^2$ and the finite-population summaries in the form used here are those of W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977, ch. 2.

title: Treatment Contrast
informal: A treatment contrast is a coefficient vector $l=(l_t)_t$ such that $$\sum_t l_t=0.$$
summary: A zero-sum coefficient vector on the treatments, evaluated at treatment means to give a comparison insensitive to the overall level.
leanSignature:
structure Contrast (T : Type*) [Fintype T] where
  coeff : T → ℝ
  sum_coeff_eq_zero : ∑ t, coeff t = 0

hypotheses.label: zero-sum coefficients
hypotheses.note: The comparison coefficients sum to zero over the treatments, $\sum_t l_t = 0$.

formalizationNotes: The zero-sum condition is a field of the structure rather than a side hypothesis: without it the object is not a contrast in Mead's sense and level-insensitivity fails, so every downstream result would have to re-assume it. Over an empty treatment set every coefficient vector is a contrast and every comparison evaluates to $0$; no nondegeneracy hypothesis is imposed. Following Mead §4.7, where no restriction is placed on the size of the coefficients, no normalisation is built in, so the contrasts form an $\mathbb R$-module rather than a normalised family.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The definitive treatment of contrasts, their estimability, their decomposition into orthogonal components and simultaneous inference about them is H. Scheffé, *The Analysis of Variance*, Wiley, New York, 1959, ch. 1 and ch. 3.

title: A Contrast Ignores the Overall Treatment Level
informal: Let $l$ be a treatment contrast, that is a coefficient vector on the treatments with $\sum_t l_t = 0$, evaluated at a family of treatment means $\mu$ as the comparison $L(\mu) = \sum_t l_t\,\mu_t$. Shifting every treatment mean by one and the same constant $a$ leaves the comparison unchanged: $$\sum_t l_t\,(\mu_t + a) = \sum_t l_t\,\mu_t.$$
summary: Adding a common constant to every treatment mean leaves a zero-sum comparison unchanged.
leanSignature:
theorem eval_add_const (c : Contrast T) (μ : T → ℝ) (a : ℝ) :
    c.eval (fun t => μ t + a) = c.eval μ

hypotheses.label: contrast
hypotheses.note: The coefficient vector sums to zero over the treatments, $\sum_t l_t = 0$.

formalizationNotes: The zero-sum condition travels with the coefficient vector as a field of the `Contrast` structure, so it appears in the type of the argument rather than as a separate hypothesis of the theorem. Proved alongside are the vanishing of the comparison on constant families, its additivity and homogeneity in the treatment means, and its additivity and homogeneity in the contrast itself.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: That the least-squares estimate of a zero-sum comparison is free of the general mean is the elementary case of the estimability theory of linear models, set out systematically in H. Scheffé, *The Analysis of Variance*, Wiley, New York, 1959, ch. 1.

title: The Completely Randomized Design
informal: Fix a finite population of $N$ units, a finite set of treatments, and a replication pattern $r$ prescribing that treatment $t$ be given to exactly $r_t$ units, where the replications exhaust the population, $\sum_t r_t = N$. An allocation assigns one treatment to each unit; the arm of $t$ under an allocation $a$ is the set $\{i : a(i) = t\}$ of units receiving $t$, and $a$ is valid for $r$ when every arm has the prescribed size. The completely randomized design is the uniform distribution on the valid allocations, $$D_r = \operatorname{Uniform}(\mathcal A_r), \qquad \mathcal A_r = \{a : |\{i : a(i) = t\}| = r_t \text{ for every } t\}.$$
summary: The uniform distribution over the allocations whose treatment-arm sizes match a prescribed replication pattern.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def completeRandomization (r : T → ℕ)
    (hr : ∑ t, r t = Fintype.card U) : RandomizationDesign U T :=
  PMF.uniformOfFinset (validAllocations r) (validAllocations_nonempty r hr)

hypotheses.label: exhaustive replications
hypotheses.note: The prescribed replications sum to the population size, $\sum_t r_t = N$.

formalizationNotes: Randomization designs are carried by Mathlib's `PMF` on the finite type of allocations rather than by a measure: expectations are then finite sums and no σ-algebra bookkeeping is needed. Nonemptiness of the support — existence of an allocation with prescribed fibre sizes — is proved by induction over the treatment set and is supplied automatically from the replication hypothesis, so the uniform law needs no further side condition. Mead §6.2 writes the replications as $n_1, \dots, n_t$.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: Physical randomization of the treatment allocation, as the device that justifies the subsequent analysis, is due to R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments*, Oliver & Boyd, Edinburgh, 1935, ch. II–III. The companion fixed-population model of the unit responses is J. Neyman's, “On the application of probability theory to agricultural experiments. Essay on principles. Section 9” (1923), translated in *Statistical Science* **5** (1990), 465–472.

title: First-Order Assignment Probability under Complete Randomization
informal: The completely randomized design with replication pattern $r$ draws an allocation uniformly at random from those assignments of the $N$ population units to treatments whose arm sizes are exactly $r$, that is from $\mathcal A_r = \{a : |\{i : a(i) = t\}| = r_t \text{ for every } t\}$; this requires the replications to exhaust the units, $\sum_t r_t = N$. Write $\chi_{t,i}(a) = \mathbf 1\{a(i) = t\}$ for the assignment indicator of unit $i$ and treatment $t$. Then for every unit and every treatment $$\mathbb E\bigl[\chi_{t,i}\bigr] = \mathbb P\bigl(a(i) = t\bigr) = \frac{r_t}{N}.$$
summary: Under complete randomization each unit receives treatment t with probability r_t/N, its allocation frequency.
leanSignature:
theorem expect_armIndicator (r : T → ℕ) (hr : ∑ t, r t = Fintype.card U)
    (i : U) (t : T) :
    pmfExpect (completeRandomization r hr) (armIndicator t i)
      = (r t : ℝ) / (Fintype.card U : ℝ)

hypotheses.label: exhaustive replications
hypotheses.note: The prescribed replications sum to the population size, $\sum_t r_t = N$.

formalizationNotes: The proof is by symmetry, not by counting: precomposition with a permutation of the units is a bijection of the valid allocations, so the marginal is the same for every unit, and summing the arm-size identity $\sum_i \chi_{t,i}(a) = r_t$ over the units identifies the common value. The cardinality of the allocation set is never computed. Division by $N$ needs no side condition, since the presence of a unit argument already forces $N \ge 1$.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The requirement that the random allocation give every unit the same chance of receiving each treatment is the starting point of the randomization theory of R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments*, Oliver & Boyd, Edinburgh, 1935; its finite-population moment calculus is developed by O. Kempthorne, *The Design and Analysis of Experiments*, Wiley, New York, 1952, ch. 8.

title: Second-Order Assignment Probability, Same Treatment
informal: The completely randomized design with replication pattern $r$ draws an allocation uniformly at random from those assignments of the $N$ population units to treatments whose arm sizes are exactly $r$, that is from $\mathcal A_r = \{a : |\{i : a(i) = t\}| = r_t \text{ for every } t\}$; this requires the replications to exhaust the units, $\sum_t r_t = N$. Write $\chi_{t,i}(a) = \mathbf 1\{a(i) = t\}$ for the assignment indicator. For two distinct units $i \ne j$ the probability that both receive the same treatment $t$ is $$\mathbb E\bigl[\chi_{t,i}\chi_{t,j}\bigr] = \mathbb P\bigl(a(i) = t,\ a(j) = t\bigr) = \frac{r_t\,(r_t - 1)}{N\,(N-1)}.$$
summary: Under complete randomization two distinct units both receive treatment t with probability r_t(r_t-1)/(N(N-1)).
leanSignature:
theorem expect_armIndicator_pair_same (r : T → ℕ)
    (hr : ∑ t, r t = Fintype.card U) {i j : U}
    (hij : i ≠ j) (t : T) :
    pmfExpect (completeRandomization r hr)
        (fun a => armIndicator t i a * armIndicator t j a)
      = (r t : ℝ) * ((r t : ℝ) - 1)
          / ((Fintype.card U : ℝ) * ((Fintype.card U : ℝ) - 1))

hypotheses.label: exhaustive replications
hypotheses.note: The prescribed replications sum to the population size, $\sum_t r_t = N$.

hypotheses.label: distinct units
hypotheses.note: The two units are different, $i \ne j$.

formalizationNotes: Distinctness of the units is needed for the displayed formula: for $i = j$ the indicator is idempotent and the expectation is the first-order probability $r_t/N$ instead. The proof again uses symmetry rather than counting — transpositions fixing $i$ show the pair moment does not depend on $j$, and summing over the units $j \ne i$ against the arm-size identity evaluates it. The denominator $N(N-1)$ never vanishes, because two distinct units force $N \ge 2$.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The calculus of first and second moments of the allocation indicators is the computational core of randomization theory as developed by O. Kempthorne, *The Design and Analysis of Experiments*, Wiley, New York, 1952, ch. 8.

title: Second-Order Assignment Probability, Distinct Treatments
informal: Under complete randomization with replication counts $r_t$ summing to $N$, for distinct units $i\ne j$ and distinct treatments $t\ne s$, $$P\{a(i)=t,\ a(j)=s\}=\frac{r_t r_s}{N(N-1)}.$$
summary: Under complete randomization distinct units receive distinct treatments t and s with probability r_t r_s/(N(N-1)).
leanSignature:
theorem expect_armIndicator_pair_distinct (r : T → ℕ)
    (hr : ∑ t, r t = Fintype.card U) {i j : U}
    (hij : i ≠ j) {t s : T}
    (hts : t ≠ s) :
    pmfExpect (completeRandomization r hr)
        (fun a => armIndicator t i a * armIndicator s j a)
      = (r t : ℝ) * (r s : ℝ)
          / ((Fintype.card U : ℝ) * ((Fintype.card U : ℝ) - 1))

hypotheses.label: exhaustive replications
hypotheses.note: The prescribed replications sum to the population size, $\sum_t r_t = N$.

hypotheses.label: distinct units
hypotheses.note: The two units are different, $i \ne j$.

hypotheses.label: distinct treatments
hypotheses.note: The two treatments are different, $t \ne s$.

formalizationNotes: Both distinctness hypotheses are needed for the displayed value. For $t = s$ the answer is the same-treatment probability $r_t(r_t-1)/(N(N-1))$, and for $i = j$ with $t \ne s$ the two arms are mutually exclusive so the probability is $0$; the formalization states those cases separately rather than absorbing them here. As in the same-treatment case, $N(N-1) \ne 0$ follows from the existence of two distinct units.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The joint distribution of the allocation indicators under a completely randomized design is the finite-population sampling calculus applied to treatment assignment; its systematic development is O. Kempthorne, *The Design and Analysis of Experiments*, Wiley, New York, 1952, ch. 8.

title: Variance of an Assignment Indicator
informal: The completely randomized design with replication pattern $r$ draws an allocation uniformly at random from those assignments of the $N$ population units to treatments whose arm sizes are exactly $r$, that is from $\mathcal A_r = \{a : |\{i : a(i) = t\}| = r_t \text{ for every } t\}$; this requires the replications to exhaust the units, $\sum_t r_t = N$. The assignment indicator $\chi_{t,i}(a) = \mathbf 1\{a(i) = t\}$ of a single unit is a Bernoulli variable with success probability $r_t/N$, so its design variance is $$\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\chi_{t,i}\bigr) = \frac{r_t}{N}\Bigl(1 - \frac{r_t}{N}\Bigr) = \frac{r_t\,(N - r_t)}{N^2}.$$
summary: An assignment indicator under complete randomization has Bernoulli variance r_t(N-r_t)/N^2.
leanSignature:
theorem var_armIndicator (r : T → ℕ) (hr : ∑ t, r t = Fintype.card U)
    (i : U) (t : T) :
    pmfVar (completeRandomization r hr) (armIndicator t i)
      = (r t : ℝ) * ((Fintype.card U : ℝ) - (r t : ℝ)) / (Fintype.card U : ℝ) ^ 2

hypotheses.label: exhaustive replications
hypotheses.note: The prescribed replications sum to the population size, $\sum_t r_t = N$.

formalizationNotes: The design variance is defined in centred form, $\mathbb E[(f - \mathbb E f)^2]$, and the computational form $\mathbb E[f^2] - (\mathbb E f)^2$ is derived rather than taken as the definition, so that nonnegativity is immediate. The proof here is that computational form together with idempotence of the indicator and the first-order assignment probability; no new counting is involved.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: Moments of the allocation indicators in the finite randomization model are developed by O. Kempthorne, *The Design and Analysis of Experiments*, Wiley, New York, 1952, ch. 8.

title: Assignments to Distinct Units Are Negatively Correlated
informal: The completely randomized design with replication pattern $r$ draws an allocation uniformly at random from those assignments of the $N$ population units to treatments whose arm sizes are exactly $r$, that is from $\mathcal A_r = \{a : |\{i : a(i) = t\}| = r_t \text{ for every } t\}$; this requires the replications to exhaust the units, $\sum_t r_t = N$. For two distinct units $i \ne j$ the assignment indicators $\chi_{t,i}(a) = \mathbf 1\{a(i) = t\}$ and $\chi_{t,j}$ of the same treatment have covariance $$\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(\chi_{t,i}, \chi_{t,j}\bigr) = -\,\frac{r_t\,(N - r_t)}{N^2\,(N-1)} = -\,\frac{1}{N-1}\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\chi_{t,i}\bigr).$$
summary: Fixed arm sizes make assignments of distinct units negatively dependent, with covariance -r_t(N-r_t)/(N^2(N-1)).
leanSignature:
theorem cov_armIndicator_of_ne (r : T → ℕ) (hr : ∑ t, r t = Fintype.card U)
    {i j : U}
    (hij : i ≠ j) (t : T) :
    pmfCov (completeRandomization r hr) (armIndicator t i) (armIndicator t j)
      = -((r t : ℝ) * ((Fintype.card U : ℝ) - (r t : ℝ)))
          / ((Fintype.card U : ℝ) ^ 2 * ((Fintype.card U : ℝ) - 1))

hypotheses.label: exhaustive replications
hypotheses.note: The prescribed replications sum to the population size, $\sum_t r_t = N$.

hypotheses.label: distinct units
hypotheses.note: The two units are different, $i \ne j$.

formalizationNotes: Distinctness of the units is required: for $i = j$ the covariance is the variance $r_t(N - r_t)/N^2$, which is stated separately. The identity is pure algebra from the first- and second-order assignment probabilities via the computational form $\operatorname{Cov}(f, g) = \mathbb E[fg] - \mathbb E[f]\,\mathbb E[g]$; the denominator $N^2(N-1)$ is nonzero because two distinct units force $N \ge 2$.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: Negative dependence of allocation indicators under fixed replication is the experimental-design counterpart of the negative covariance of inclusion indicators in sampling without replacement; see W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977, ch. 2, and O. Kempthorne, *The Design and Analysis of Experiments*, Wiley, New York, 1952, ch. 8.

title: Marginal Assignment Probability under Blocked Randomization
informal: A blocked randomization groups the population units into blocks by a labelling $b(\cdot)$ and runs an independent completely randomized design inside each block, treatment $t$ being given to $r_b(t)$ of the $N_b$ units of block $b$; this requires the within-block replications to exhaust each block, $\sum_t r_b(t) = N_b$ for every $b$. The randomized complete block design of the textbooks is the equireplicate case $r_b(t) = 1$. The per-block allocations are glued into a single allocation of the whole population. Then a unit $i$ receives treatment $t$ with the allocation frequency of its own block, $$\mathbb P\bigl(a(i) = t\bigr) = \frac{r_{b(i)}(t)}{N_{b(i)}}.$$
summary: Under blocked randomization a unit receives treatment t with the allocation frequency of its own block.
leanSignature:
theorem blocked_expect_armIndicator (bl : U → B) (r : B → T → ℕ)
    (hr : ∀ b, ∑ t, r b t = Fintype.card (Stratum bl b)) (i : U) (t : T) :
    pmfExpect (blockedRandomization bl r hr)
        (fun ω => armIndicator t i (glueAllocation bl ω))
      = (r (bl i) t : ℝ) / (Fintype.card (Stratum bl (bl i)) : ℝ)

hypotheses.label: blockwise exhaustive replications
hypotheses.note: Within every block the prescribed replications sum to the block size, $\sum_t r_b(t) = N_b$.

formalizationNotes: The sample space is the dependent product of the per-block allocation spaces, blocks being modelled as subtypes of the population; a unit's own block therefore contains it by construction and the displayed denominator is never zero. The proof composes the marginal identity for a product design with the first-order assignment probability of the within-block completely randomized design. Deeper blocked moments — within-block pair probabilities and blocked arm means — are not part of this statement.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: Restricted randomization within blocks is introduced in R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments*, Oliver & Boyd, Edinburgh, 1935, ch. IV, and analysed in the finite model by O. Kempthorne, *The Design and Analysis of Experiments*, Wiley, New York, 1952, ch. 9.

title: Assignments in Different Blocks Are Uncorrelated
informal: Suppose independent complete randomizations are performed within blocks, with the treatment counts in each block summing to that block's size. If units $i$ and $j$ lie in different blocks, then for any treatments $t$ and $s$, $$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\mathbf 1\{a(i)=t\},\mathbf 1\{a(j)=s\}\right)=0.$$
summary: Assignment indicators of units in different blocks have zero covariance, killing cross-block terms in design variances.
leanSignature:
