theorem blocked_cov_armIndicator_of_ne_block (bl : U → B) (r : B → T → ℕ)
    (hr : ∀ b, ∑ t, r b t = Fintype.card (Stratum bl b)) {i j : U}
    (hij : bl i ≠ bl j) (t s : T) :
    pmfCov (blockedRandomization bl r hr)
        (fun ω => armIndicator t i (glueAllocation bl ω))
        (fun ω => armIndicator s j (glueAllocation bl ω)) = 0

hypotheses.label: blockwise exhaustive replications
hypotheses.note: Within every block the prescribed replications sum to the block size, $\sum_t r_b(t) = N_b$.

hypotheses.label: distinct blocks
hypotheses.note: The two units carry different block labels, $b(i) \ne b(j)$.

formalizationNotes: That the blocks differ is essential: within one block the assignments are those of a completely randomized design and are negatively correlated. The result is an instance of the general fact that statistics of distinct components of a product design are uncorrelated, which is proved once and reused by the stratified sampling estimators.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: Independence of the randomization across blocks, and its role in eliminating cross-block covariance terms, is the analysis of O. Kempthorne, *The Design and Analysis of Experiments*, Wiley, New York, 1952, ch. 9.

title: The One-Way Analysis of Variance Identity
informal: Let $y$ be the observed data on the units of a completed one-way experiment and let $g$ be the treatment assignment actually used, so that unit $i$ received treatment $g(i)$. Write $\bar y$ for the grand mean and $\bar y_t$ for the mean of the arm of $t$, that is of the units assigned to $t$. Then the total variation about the grand mean splits exactly into a between-treatment and a within-treatment part: $$\underbrace{\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2}_{SS_{\mathrm{Total}}} = \underbrace{\sum_i (\bar y_{g(i)} - \bar y)^2}_{SS_{\mathrm{Treatment}}} + \underbrace{\sum_i (y_i - \bar y_{g(i)})^2}_{SS_{\mathrm{Residual}}}.$$
summary: Total variation about the grand mean equals between-treatment plus within-treatment variation, for every treatment assignment.
leanSignature:
theorem anova_decomposition (y : U → ℝ) (g : Allocation U T) :
    totalSS y = treatmentSS y g + residualSS y g
formalizationNotes: The treatment and residual sums of squares are written as sums over units rather than over treatment groups. Since the arm of $g(i)$ always contains $i$, no empty group is ever averaged over, and the identity therefore holds with no nonemptiness or positive-replication hypothesis at all. The grouped form $SS_{\mathrm{Treatment}} = \sum_t n_t (\bar y_t - \bar y)^2$ is stated separately. Only the algebra of the decomposition belongs here; the associated distribution theory (chi-squared and $F$ laws) lives in the hypothesis-testing area.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The partition of the sum of squares is R. A. Fisher's, *Statistical Methods for Research Workers*, Oliver & Boyd, Edinburgh, 1925; the definitive modern account of the algebra and its distribution theory is H. Scheffé, *The Analysis of Variance*, Wiley, New York, 1959, ch. 2–3.

title: Grouped Form of the Treatment Sum of Squares
informal: Let $y$ be the observed data on the units of a one-way experiment with treatment assignment $g$, let $\bar y$ be the grand mean, and for each treatment $t$ let $n_t$ be the number of units assigned to $t$ and $\bar y_t$ the mean of those units. The between-treatment sum of squares, defined as a sum over units of the squared deviation of each unit's own arm mean from the grand mean, collapses to the familiar replication-weighted sum over treatments: $$\sum_i \bigl(\bar y_{g(i)} - \bar y\bigr)^2 = \sum_t n_t \bigl(\bar y_t - \bar y\bigr)^2.$$
summary: The between-treatment sum of squares equals the replication-weighted sum of squared arm-mean deviations from the grand mean.
leanSignature:
theorem treatmentSS_eq_sum_card (y : U → ℝ) (g : Allocation U T) :
    treatmentSS y g
      = ∑ t, ((arm t g).card : ℝ) * (armMean y t g - populationMean y) ^ 2
formalizationNotes: The unit-indexed definition is taken as primary and the grouped form derived, so that no empty-group averaging convention is ever exercised: a treatment with $n_t = 0$ contributes a term of weight $0$ on the right-hand side and does not appear at all on the left. The identity therefore needs no positive-replication hypothesis.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The analysis-of-variance table of a completely randomized design, with its treatment line in this weighted form, is standard; see H. Scheffé, *The Analysis of Variance*, Wiley, New York, 1959, ch. 3.

title: Orthogonality of Two-Level Factorial Characters
informal: For a two-level factorial design, define $\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j$ for each set of factors $S$ and level vector $x\in\{-1,1\}^k$. Then $$\sum_x\chi_S(x)\chi_T(x)=\begin{cases}2^k,&S=T,\\0,&S\ne T.\end{cases}$$
summary: Distinct two-level factorial characters are orthogonal over the treatment combinations, each having squared length 2^k.
leanSignature:
theorem sum_character_mul (S T : Finset ι) :
    ∑ x : ι → Bool, character S x * character T x
      = if S = T then (2 : ℝ) ^ Fintype.card ι else 0
formalizationNotes: Level vectors are encoded as Boolean functions on the factor index, with the sign map sending `true` to $+1$ and `false` to $-1$, so the factor index may be an arbitrary finite type rather than `Fin k`; $2^k$ then appears as the cardinality of the function type. The proof is multiplicativity of characters together with the vanishing of the sum of any nonempty-set character, using that the symmetric difference is empty exactly when the two sets agree.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The $\pm 1$ effect matrix with orthogonal rows, and the product rule for interaction rows, are the calculus of F. Yates, *The Design and Analysis of Factorial Experiments*, Imperial Bureau of Soil Science, Harpenden, 1937, built on the factorial principle of R. A. Fisher, *The Design of Experiments*, Oliver & Boyd, Edinburgh, 1935, ch. VI.

title: The Factorial Expansion of a Two-Level Response
informal: For a response $y$ on the level vectors $x\in\{-1,1\}^k$, define $$\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j,\qquad \widehat y(S)=2^{-k}\sum_x y(x)\chi_S(x).$$ Then every response satisfies $$y(x)=\sum_S\widehat y(S)\chi_S(x).$$
summary: Every response on a two-level factorial is the character sum of its factorial coefficients, and those coefficients are unique.
leanSignature:
theorem factorialExpansion (y : (ι → Bool) → ℝ) (x : ι → Bool) :
    y x = ∑ S : Finset ι, factorialCoeff y S * character S x
formalizationNotes: The normalisation differs from the book's, deliberately. Mead scales an $m$-factor effect by $1/2^{m-1}$ and the overall mean by $1/2^m$, whereas the factorial coefficient formalized here uses $2^{-k}$ uniformly; a Mead effect is therefore twice the coefficient used here for a nonempty effect set, while the coefficient at the empty set is exactly Mead's overall mean. The uniform normalisation is what makes the expansion, its uniqueness and the Parseval identity clean, and consumers are expected to convert. Mathematically the block is finite Fourier inversion on the Boolean cube in elementary dress.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The representation of a factorial response by its effects, and the recovery of the effects from the response by the $\pm 1$ contrasts, is due to F. Yates, *The Design and Analysis of Factorial Experiments*, Imperial Bureau of Soil Science, Harpenden, 1937; the reading of the same calculus as finite Fourier analysis on $(\mathbb Z/2)^k$ is now standard in the design literature.

title: Sum-of-Squares Decomposition of a Two-Level Factorial
informal: For a response $y$ on the level vectors $x\in\{-1,1\}^k$, let $\widehat y(S)=2^{-k}\sum_x y(x)\chi_S(x)$, where $\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j$. Then $$\sum_x y(x)^2=2^k\sum_S\widehat y(S)^2.$$
summary: The total sum of squares of a two-level factorial response is 2^k times the sum of squared factorial coefficients.
leanSignature:
theorem factorialParseval (y : (ι → Bool) → ℝ) :
    ∑ x, y x ^ 2
      = (2 : ℝ) ^ Fintype.card ι * ∑ S : Finset ι, factorialCoeff y S ^ 2
formalizationNotes: As for the expansion, the coefficients are normalised uniformly by $2^{-k}$ rather than by Mead's $1/2^{m-1}$ for an $m$-factor effect, so a component attributed to the effect $S$ here is $2^k \widehat y(S)^2$ and must be rescaled before being compared with a component computed from Mead-scaled effects. The sum on the left runs over the $2^k$ treatment combinations, so this is the single-replicate identity; with replication the residual line comes from the replicate structure and is not part of this statement.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The decomposition of a factorial sum of squares into single-degree-of-freedom effect components is due to F. Yates, *The Design and Analysis of Factorial Experiments*, Imperial Bureau of Soil Science, Harpenden, 1937; its place in the general theory of orthogonal decompositions is set out in H. Scheffé, *The Analysis of Variance*, Wiley, New York, 1959, ch. 4.

title: Inclusion Probabilities of a Sampling Design
informal: For a sampling design that draws a random subset $S$ of a finite population, the first-order inclusion probability of unit $i$ is $$\pi_i=P(i\in S)=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbf 1\{i\in S\}\right].$$
summary: The probabilities that a unit, or a pair of units, falls in the random sample drawn by a sampling design.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def inclusionProb (D : SamplingDesign U) (i : U) : ℝ :=
  pmfExpect D (inclusionIndicator i)
formalizationNotes: A sampling design is a probability mass function on the finite type of subsets of the population, so every quantity here is a finite sum and the bounds follow from monotonicity of the design expectation against the constants $0$ and $1$. No positivity of $\pi_i$ is assumed at this level; it enters only for the Horvitz–Thompson estimator downstream, where dividing by $\pi_i$ requires it.

reference.formal: D. G. Horvitz and D. J. Thompson, “A generalization of sampling without replacement from a finite universe,” *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **47** (1952), 663–685.
reference.biblio: The textbook development of the inclusion-probability calculus, including the second-order probabilities and the variance kernel, is W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977, ch. 9A, and C.-E. Särndal, B. Swensson and J. Wretman, *Model Assisted Survey Sampling*, Springer, New York, 1992, ch. 2.

title: The Horvitz–Thompson Estimator
informal: If a sampling design has inclusion probabilities $\pi_i=P(i\in S)$, the Horvitz–Thompson estimator of the population total $\sum_i y_i$ is $$\widehat Y_{\mathrm{HT}}(S)=\sum_{i\in S}\frac{y_i}{\pi_i}.$$
summary: The estimator of a population total that weights each sampled value by the reciprocal of its inclusion probability.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def horvitzThompson (D : SamplingDesign U) (y : U → ℝ)
    (s : Finset U) : ℝ :=
  ∑ i ∈ s, y i / inclusionProb D i
formalizationNotes: The estimator itself carries no positivity hypothesis: a unit with $\pi_i = 0$ contributes $y_i / 0 = 0$ under Lean's division convention, and such a unit is in any case never observed. Positivity of every $\pi_i$ — a measurable design, in the survey-sampling sense — is imposed explicitly on the moment theorems, where it is a genuine condition and not a convention, since without it the values of the unreachable units cannot be estimated at all.

reference.formal: D. G. Horvitz and D. J. Thompson, “A generalization of sampling without replacement from a finite universe,” *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **47** (1952), 663–685.
reference.biblio: The systematic development of inverse-probability weighting, together with alternative variance estimators, is W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977, ch. 9A, and C.-E. Särndal, B. Swensson and J. Wretman, *Model Assisted Survey Sampling*, Springer, New York, 1992, ch. 2.

title: Design Unbiasedness of the Horvitz–Thompson Estimator
informal: Let a sampling design on a finite population draw a random sample $S$, with first-order inclusion probabilities $\pi_i = \mathbb P(i \in S)$, and let $y$ be a fixed quantity on the units. If every unit has a positive inclusion probability, $\pi_i > 0$, then the Horvitz–Thompson estimator $\widehat Y_{\mathrm{HT}}(S) = \sum_{i \in S} y_i / \pi_i$ is exactly unbiased for the population total: $$\mathbb E\bigl[\widehat Y_{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr] = \sum_{i} y_i.$$
summary: With positive inclusion probabilities the Horvitz-Thompson estimator has design expectation equal to the population total.
leanSignature:
theorem horvitzThompson_unbiased (D : SamplingDesign U) (y : U → ℝ)
    (hpos : ∀ i, 0 < inclusionProb D i) :
    pmfExpect D (horvitzThompson D y) = populationTotal y

hypotheses.label: positive inclusion probabilities
hypotheses.note: Every unit is reachable by the design: $\pi_i > 0$ for all $i$.

formalizationNotes: Positivity of the inclusion probabilities is a genuine hypothesis rather than a technicality: units with $\pi_i = 0$ are never observed and their contribution to the total cannot be recovered. The proof is the indicator representation of the estimator together with linearity of the design expectation and $\mathbb E[\mathbf 1\{i \in S\}] = \pi_i$; the population total on the right is a function of the data alone, never of the design.

reference.formal: D. G. Horvitz and D. J. Thompson, “A generalization of sampling without replacement from a finite universe,” *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **47** (1952), 663–685.
reference.biblio: Design unbiasedness under arbitrary unequal-probability sampling is what established inverse-probability weighting as the default estimator of a finite-population total; its textbook treatment is W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977, ch. 9A, and the same weighting underlies the missing-data theory begun by D. B. Rubin, “Inference and missing data,” *Biometrika* **63** (1976), 581–592.

title: Exact Design Variance of the Horvitz–Thompson Estimator
informal: Let a sampling design on a finite population draw a random sample $S$, with inclusion probabilities $\pi_i = \mathbb P(i \in S)$ and $\pi_{ij} = \mathbb P(i \in S,\ j \in S)$, the latter with the diagonal convention $\pi_{ii} = \pi_i$. If every unit has a positive inclusion probability, $\pi_i > 0$, the design variance of the Horvitz–Thompson estimator $\widehat Y_{\mathrm{HT}}(S) = \sum_{i \in S} y_i / \pi_i$ is exactly $$\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\widehat Y_{\mathrm{HT}}\bigr) = \sum_{i}\sum_{j} \frac{\pi_{ij} - \pi_i \pi_j}{\pi_i \pi_j}\, y_i y_j.$$
summary: The exact design variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator in terms of first- and second-order inclusion probabilities.
leanSignature:
theorem horvitzThompson_variance (D : SamplingDesign U) (y : U → ℝ)
    (hpos : ∀ i, 0 < inclusionProb D i) :
    pmfVar D (horvitzThompson D y)
      = ∑ i, ∑ j,
          (pairInclusionProb D i j - inclusionProb D i * inclusionProb D j)
            / (inclusionProb D i * inclusionProb D j) * (y i * y j)

hypotheses.label: positive inclusion probabilities
hypotheses.note: Every unit is reachable by the design: $\pi_i > 0$ for all $i$.

formalizationNotes: The variance is stated in the double-sum form, with the diagonal included through the convention $\pi_{ii} = \pi_i$, rather than in the Sen–Yates–Grundy form, which is equivalent to it only for fixed-size designs; the statement here holds for an arbitrary design with positive inclusion probabilities and possibly random sample size. It is derived from the general expansion of the variance of a sum into a double sum of covariances, together with the inclusion-indicator covariance $\pi_{ij} - \pi_i\pi_j$.

reference.formal: D. G. Horvitz and D. J. Thompson, “A generalization of sampling without replacement from a finite universe,” *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **47** (1952), 663–685.
reference.biblio: An alternative and often more stable expression for fixed-size designs is due to A. R. Sen, “On the estimate of the variance in sampling with varying probabilities,” *Journal of the Indian Society of Agricultural Statistics* **5** (1953), 119–127, and independently to F. Yates and P. M. Grundy, “Selection without replacement from within strata with probability proportional to size,” *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B* **15** (1953), 253–261; both are discussed in W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977, ch. 9A.

title: Inclusion Probabilities under Simple Random Sampling
informal: Under simple random sampling without replacement of $n$ units from a population of $N$ units, with $n\le N$, every unit has inclusion probability $$\pi_i=P(i\in S)=\frac nN.$$
summary: Simple random sampling without replacement includes each unit with probability n/N and each pair with probability n(n-1)/(N(N-1)).
leanSignature:
theorem srs_inclusionProb (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≤ Fintype.card U) (i : U) :
    inclusionProb (simpleRandomSampling n hn) i
      = (n : ℝ) / (Fintype.card U : ℝ)

hypotheses.label: feasible sample size
hypotheses.note: The sample size does not exceed the population size, $n \le N$.

formalizationNotes: The sample-size hypothesis is what makes the family of $n$-element subsets nonempty, so that the uniform law exists; it is carried by the design itself and therefore reappears in every statement about it. Both inclusion probabilities are proved by relabelling symmetry rather than by counting subsets: a permutation of the units leaves the design invariant, forcing the first-order probabilities to be equal and the second-order ones to be equal off the diagonal, and the expected sample size $\sum_i \pi_i = n$ then pins down the common values. The pair formula is stated for distinct units; the diagonal is $\pi_{ii} = \pi_i$ by convention. The scaled-sample-total form of the Horvitz–Thompson estimator is proved pointwise, for every subset rather than only those in the support.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The inclusion probabilities of simple random sampling without replacement and their consequences are classical; see W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977, ch. 2, and, for the reduction of the inverse-probability estimator to the scaled sample total, D. G. Horvitz and D. J. Thompson, “A generalization of sampling without replacement from a finite universe,” *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **47** (1952), 663–685.

title: Unbiasedness of the Sample Mean under Simple Random Sampling
informal: Simple random sampling without replacement of size $n$ from a finite population of $N$ units draws a subset uniformly at random from all subsets of exactly $n$ units, which requires the sample size not to exceed the population size, $n \le N$. Assume also that the sample size is positive, $n \ne 0$, so that the sample mean $\bar y_S = n^{-1}\sum_{i \in S} y_i$ is well defined. Then the sample mean is exactly unbiased for the population mean: $$\mathbb E\bigl[\bar y_S\bigr] = \bar y = \frac1N \sum_{i} y_i.$$
summary: Under simple random sampling without replacement the sample mean has design expectation equal to the population mean.
leanSignature:
theorem srs_sampleMean_unbiased (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≤ Fintype.card U)
    (hn0 : n ≠ 0) (y : U → ℝ) :
    pmfExpect (simpleRandomSampling n hn) (sampleMean y) = populationMean y

hypotheses.label: feasible sample size
hypotheses.note: The sample size does not exceed the population size, $n \le N$.

hypotheses.label: positive sample size
hypotheses.note: The sample size is nonzero, $n \ne 0$, so the sample mean is well defined.

formalizationNotes: The positive-sample-size hypothesis is needed because the sample mean is defined with the convention that the mean over an empty sample is $0$: for $n = 0$ the left-hand side would be $0$ while the population mean need not be. On the support of the design the sample mean is the linear statistic $n^{-1}\sum_i \mathbf 1\{i \in S\}\,y_i$, and the result follows from the first-order inclusion probability $n/N$.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: Unbiasedness of the sample mean under simple random sampling without replacement is W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977, ch. 2, Theorem 2.1.

title: Finite-Population Correction for the Sample Mean
informal: Simple random sampling without replacement of size $n$ from a finite population of $N$ units draws a subset uniformly at random from all subsets of exactly $n$ units, which requires the sample size not to exceed the population size, $n \le N$. Assume also that the sample size is positive, $n \ne 0$, so that the sample mean $\bar y_S = n^{-1}\sum_{i \in S} y_i$ is well defined, and let $S^2_y = (N-1)^{-1}\sum_i (y_i - \bar y)^2$ be the finite-population variance of the unit values. Then the design variance of the sample mean is exactly $$\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\bar y_S\bigr) = \Bigl(1 - \frac nN\Bigr)\frac{S^2_y}{n}.$$
summary: The design variance of the sample mean under sampling without replacement is (1-n/N) times the population variance over n.
leanSignature:
theorem srs_sampleMean_variance (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≤ Fintype.card U)
    (hn0 : n ≠ 0) (y : U → ℝ) :
    pmfVar (simpleRandomSampling n hn) (sampleMean y)
      = (1 - (n : ℝ) / (Fintype.card U : ℝ)) * populationVariance y / (n : ℝ)

hypotheses.label: feasible sample size
hypotheses.note: The sample size does not exceed the population size, $n \le N$.

hypotheses.label: positive sample size
hypotheses.note: The sample size is nonzero, $n \ne 0$, so the sample mean is well defined.

formalizationNotes: The identity is exact rather than asymptotic, and $S^2_y$ carries the $N-1$ normalisation; with an $N$ normalisation the correction factor would read $(N-n)/(N-1)$ instead. Degenerate cases are covered rather than excluded: for $n = N$ both sides vanish, and for $N = 1$, which forces $n = 1$, the sample is deterministic and both sides are zero, so nothing beyond a positive, feasible sample size is assumed. The proof expands the variance of the linear statistic into the double sum of inclusion covariances and evaluates it with the first- and second-order inclusion probabilities.

reference.formal: R. Mead, *The Design of Experiments: Statistical Principles for Practical Applications*, Cambridge University Press, 1988.
reference.biblio: The finite-population correction and the exact variance of the mean under sampling without replacement are W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977, ch. 2, Theorem 2.2.

title: Unbiasedness of the Stratified Sample Mean
informal: Stratified simple random sampling partitions a population of $N$ units into strata by a labelling, the stratum of label $b$ having $N_b$ units, and draws an independent simple random sample without replacement of size $n_b$ inside each stratum; this requires each within-stratum sample size to be feasible, $n_b \le N_b$. The stratified estimator of the population mean is the size-weighted combination of the within-stratum sample means, $$\widehat{\bar y} = \sum_b \frac{N_b}{N}\, \bar y_{S_b}.$$ Assume in addition that every stratum is sampled, $n_b \ne 0$ for each $b$, and that the population is nonempty. Then the stratified estimator is exactly unbiased for the population mean: $$\mathbb E\Bigl[\sum_b \frac{N_b}{N}\,\bar y_{S_b}\Bigr] = \bar y = \frac1N \sum_{i} y_i.$$
summary: The size-weighted combination of within-stratum sample means is design-unbiased for the population mean.
leanSignature:
theorem stratifiedSRS_mean_unbiased
    [Nonempty U] (st : U → B) (n : B → ℕ)
    (hn : ∀ b, n b ≤ Fintype.card (Stratum st b))
    (hpos : ∀ b, n b ≠ 0) (y : U → ℝ) :
    pmfExpect (stratifiedSRS st n hn) (stratifiedMeanEstimator st y)
      = populationMean y

hypotheses.label: nonempty population
hypotheses.note: The population has at least one unit, so the population size $N$ is invertible.

hypotheses.label: feasible stratum sample sizes
hypotheses.note: Within every stratum the sample size does not exceed the stratum size, $n_b \le N_b$.

hypotheses.label: every stratum sampled
hypotheses.note: Every stratum receives a positive sample size, $n_b \ne 0$.

formalizationNotes: Two hypotheses are added relative to a bare textbook statement, and both are honest side conditions of the formal version. Nonemptiness of the population is needed only so that $N$ can be inverted; the empty case would read $0 = 0$, but the proof divides by $N$. Requiring $n_b \ne 0$ in every stratum forces, through $n_b \le N_b$, every stratum to be nonempty, which is the textbook stratified frame; a version admitting empty strata would have to drop their weight-zero terms and is not formalized. Strata are modelled as subtypes of the population, so a within-stratum summary is literally the finite-population summary of the restricted quantity.

reference.formal: W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977.
reference.biblio: Stratification as a variance-reduction device, and the optimal allocation of a fixed total sample size across strata, are due to J. Neyman, “On the two different aspects of the representative method: the method of stratified sampling and the method of purposive selection,” *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society* **97** (1934), 558–625.

title: Exact Variance of the Stratified Sample Mean
informal: Stratified simple random sampling partitions a population of $N$ units into strata by a labelling, the stratum of label $b$ having $N_b$ units, and draws an independent simple random sample without replacement of size $n_b$ inside each stratum; this requires each within-stratum sample size to be feasible, $n_b \le N_b$. The stratified estimator of the population mean is the size-weighted combination of the within-stratum sample means, $$\widehat{\bar y} = \sum_b \frac{N_b}{N}\, \bar y_{S_b}.$$ Assume in addition that every stratum is sampled, $n_b \ne 0$ for each $b$, and write $S_b^2$ for the finite-population variance of the unit values inside stratum $b$. Then the design variance of the stratified estimator is exactly $$\operatorname{Var}\Bigl[\sum_b \frac{N_b}{N}\,\bar y_{S_b}\Bigr] = \sum_b \Bigl(\frac{N_b}{N}\Bigr)^{2} \Bigl(1 - \frac{n_b}{N_b}\Bigr)\frac{S_b^2}{n_b}.$$
summary: The variance of the stratified sample mean is the weighted sum of within-stratum variances, with no cross-stratum terms.
leanSignature:
theorem stratifiedSRS_mean_variance (st : U → B) (n : B → ℕ)
    (hn : ∀ b, n b ≤ Fintype.card (Stratum st b))
    (hpos : ∀ b, n b ≠ 0) (y : U → ℝ) :
    pmfVar (stratifiedSRS st n hn) (stratifiedMeanEstimator st y)
      = ∑ b, ((Fintype.card (Stratum st b) : ℝ) / (Fintype.card U : ℝ)) ^ 2
          * ((1 - (n b : ℝ) / (Fintype.card (Stratum st b) : ℝ))
              * populationVariance (fun i : Stratum st b => y i) / (n b : ℝ))

hypotheses.label: feasible stratum sample sizes
hypotheses.note: Within every stratum the sample size does not exceed the stratum size, $n_b \le N_b$.

hypotheses.label: every stratum sampled
hypotheses.note: Every stratum receives a positive sample size, $n_b \ne 0$.

formalizationNotes: Unlike the unbiasedness statement, this one needs no nonemptiness hypothesis on the population: it compares weighted variances and the degenerate weights take care of themselves. Requiring $n_b \ne 0$ in every stratum forces every stratum to be nonempty and is the textbook stratified frame; empty strata would require dropping their weight-zero terms and are not covered. The proof is the independence calculus of a product design — variances of stratum-wise sums add, with no cross-stratum covariance — instantiated at the within-stratum variance formula with its finite-population correction.

reference.formal: W. G. Cochran, *Sampling Techniques*, 3rd ed., Wiley, New York, 1977.
reference.biblio: The variance formula and the resulting theory of optimal allocation across strata are due to J. Neyman, “On the two different aspects of the representative method: the method of stratified sampling and the method of purposive selection,” *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society* **97** (1934), 558–625.

title: True Risk
informal: Fix a domain of examples $\mathcal{Z}$, a set of hypotheses, and a loss function $\ell(h,z)$ measuring the cost of using the hypothesis $h$ on the example $z$. The true risk (or generalization error) of $h$ with respect to a probability distribution $D$ on $\mathcal{Z}$ is the expected loss $$L_D(h)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{z\sim D}\bigl[\ell(h,z)\bigr]\;=\;\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\ell(h,z)\,dD(z).$$
summary: The true risk of a hypothesis is the expected loss it incurs on an example drawn from the data distribution.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def risk [MeasurableSpace Z] (D : Measure Z) (ℓ : H → Z → ℝ)
    (h : H) : ℝ :=
  ∫ z, ℓ h z ∂D
formalizationNotes: The hypotheses form an abstract type rather than a set, and the loss is a family indexed by it, so that the risk of a hypothesis outside the class one is learning is still defined. Nonnegativity and integrability of the loss are not built into the definition but appear as hypotheses of the theorems that need them: the Bochner integral returns the junk value $0$ when the loss is not integrable.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: The general loss-based (agnostic) learning setting, in which the object minimized is an expected loss over an unknown distribution, is due to D. Haussler, “Decision theoretic generalizations of the PAC model for neural net and other learning applications,” *Information and Computation* **100** (1992), 78–150, generalizing the classification model of L. G. Valiant, “A theory of the learnable,” *Communications of the ACM* **27** (1984), 1134–1142. The view of learning as risk minimization from a finite sample goes back to V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis (1971).

title: Empirical Risk
informal: A training sample of size $n$ is a finite sequence $S=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ of examples, so that order and repetitions are visible. The empirical risk (or training error) of a hypothesis $h$ on $S$ is the average loss it incurs on the sample, $$L_S(h)\;=\;\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(h,z_i).$$
summary: The empirical risk of a hypothesis is the average loss it incurs on the observed training sample.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def empRisk {n : ℕ} (ℓ : H → Z → ℝ) (s : Sample Z n) (h : H) : ℝ :=
  (n : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ i, ℓ h (s i)
formalizationNotes: A sample is a function on the index set with $n$ elements, i.e. a sequence, matching the book's convention that a training set is a sequence rather than a set. At $n = 0$ the definition returns the junk value $0$, since the inverse of $0$ is $0$ in Lean's reals; every theorem about the empirical risk therefore assumes at least one example.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: Empirical risk minimization and the study of when the empirical risk is uniformly close to the true risk originate with V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis, “On the uniform convergence of relative frequencies of events to their probabilities,” *Theory of Probability and Its Applications* **16** (1971), 264–280.

title: Empirical Risk Minimization
informal: Given a hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ and a training sample $S$, a hypothesis $h$ is an empirical risk minimizer when it belongs to the class and no member of the class has smaller empirical risk: $$h\in\mathcal{H}\quad\text{and}\quad L_S(h)\;\le\;L_S(g)\ \text{ for every } g\in\mathcal{H}.$$
summary: A hypothesis is an empirical risk minimizer when it lies in the class and attains the smallest empirical risk in it.
formalizationNotes: This is a predicate on a hypothesis, not a selection operator: existence, uniqueness, choice and measurability of a minimizer are deliberately not built in. A learning rule that returns an empirical risk minimizer enters the downstream theorems as data, together with the hypothesis that it satisfies this predicate at every sample. The approximate variant `IsApproxERM` in the same file adds the slack $\eta$, and agrees with this predicate at $\eta = 0$.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: Empirical risk minimization as an inductive principle, and the necessity of restricting the hypothesis class, are due to V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis, “On the uniform convergence of relative frequencies of events to their probabilities,” *Theory of Probability and Its Applications* **16** (1971), 264–280.

title: ε-Representative Sample
informal: A training sample $S$ is $\varepsilon$-representative for the hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$, the loss $\ell$ and the distribution $D$ when the empirical risk of every hypothesis in the class is within $\varepsilon$ of its true risk: $$\bigl|L_S(h)-L_D(h)\bigr|\;\le\;\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every }h\in\mathcal{H}.$$
summary: A sample is epsilon-representative when every hypothesis in the class has empirical risk within epsilon of its true risk.
formalizationNotes: The definition is stated with a universally quantified bound rather than as a supremum, so that no measurability or boundedness is needed for the notion itself and it makes sense for an arbitrary class. The book's supremum form is recovered from this one whenever the supremum exists.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: Uniform closeness of empirical to true frequencies over a whole class, rather than for a fixed hypothesis, is the central object of V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis, “On the uniform convergence of relative frequencies of events to their probabilities,” *Theory of Probability and Its Applications* **16** (1971), 264–280.

title: Uniform Convergence Property
informal: A hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ has the uniform convergence property with sample complexity $m^{\mathrm{UC}}$ when, for every accuracy $\varepsilon>0$ and confidence $\delta\in(0,1)$, every distribution $D$ on the example domain, and every sample size $n\ge m^{\mathrm{UC}}(\varepsilon,\delta)$, an independent sample $S$ of size $n$ drawn from $D$ satisfies $$\Pr_{S\sim D^{n}}\Bigl[\,\bigl|L_S(h)-L_D(h)\bigr|\le\varepsilon\ \text{ for every }h\in\mathcal{H}\,\Bigr]\;\ge\;1-\delta;$$ that is, the sample is $\varepsilon$-representative with probability at least $1-\delta$.
summary: A class has the uniform convergence property when a sample of the stated size is epsilon-representative with probability at least 1 minus delta, for every distribution.
leanSignature:
def HasUniformConvergenceWith [MeasurableSpace Z] (𝓗 : Set H)
    (ℓ : H → Z → ℝ) (mUC : ℝ → ℝ → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (D : Measure Z), IsProbabilityMeasure D →
    ∀ ε δ : ℝ, 0 < ε → 0 < δ → δ < 1 →
      ∀ n : ℕ, mUC ε δ ≤ n →
        ENNReal.ofReal (1 - δ) ≤
          sampleLaw D n {s | UniformDeviationLE D 𝓗 ℓ s ε}
formalizationNotes: The sample complexity is carried as an explicit witness function rather than existentially quantified, so that theorems can state the bound they achieve. The probability is taken on the raw event, without assuming it measurable: an outer-measure lower bound is a stronger statement than the same bound for a measurable event, and measurability enters only inside the proofs. The law of the sample is the $n$-fold product measure.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: Distribution-free uniform convergence as the route to learnability is due to V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis, “On the uniform convergence of relative frequencies of events to their probabilities,” *Theory of Probability and Its Applications* **16** (1971), 264–280; its role in characterizing learnable classes was developed by A. Blumer, A. Ehrenfeucht, D. Haussler and M. K. Warmuth, “Learnability and the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension,” *Journal of the ACM* **36** (1989), 929–965.

title: Agnostic PAC Learnability
informal: A learning rule $A$, which maps a sample of any size to a hypothesis, agnostically PAC-learns the class $\mathcal{H}$ for the loss $\ell$ with sample complexity $m$ when for every accuracy $\varepsilon>0$, confidence $\delta\in(0,1)$, distribution $D$ on the example domain, and sample size $n\ge m(\varepsilon,\delta)$, $$\Pr_{S\sim D^{n}}\Bigl[\,L_D\bigl(A(S)\bigr)\;\le\;\inf_{g\in\mathcal{H}}L_D(g)+\varepsilon\,\Bigr]\;\ge\;1-\delta.$$
summary: A rule agnostically PAC-learns a class when, from enough samples, it returns with high probability a hypothesis whose risk is within epsilon of the best in the class.
leanSignature:
def IsAgnosticPACLearnerWith [MeasurableSpace Z] (𝓗 : Set H)
    (ℓ : H → Z → ℝ) (A : ∀ n : ℕ, Sample Z n → H) (mSC : ℝ → ℝ → ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (D : Measure Z), IsProbabilityMeasure D →
    ∀ ε δ : ℝ, 0 < ε → 0 < δ → δ < 1 →
      ∀ n : ℕ, mSC ε δ ≤ n →
        ENNReal.ofReal (1 - δ) ≤
          sampleLaw D n {s | risk D ℓ (A n s) ≤ bestRisk D 𝓗 ℓ + ε}
formalizationNotes: The best-in-class risk is the infimum of the risk over the image of the class, which avoids the degenerate floor at $0$ that a real-valued indexed infimum would introduce; it takes the junk value $0$ for an empty class or an image unbounded below, so theorems carry nonemptiness and nonnegativity hypotheses. As with the uniform convergence property, the sample complexity is an explicit witness and the probability is a lower bound on the raw event.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: The agnostic model, in which no assumption is made about the distribution and the learner competes with the best hypothesis in the class, is due to D. Haussler, “Decision theoretic generalizations of the PAC model for neural net and other learning applications,” *Information and Computation* **100** (1992), 78–150, extending the realizable model of L. G. Valiant, “A theory of the learnable,” *Communications of the ACM* **27** (1984), 1134–1142.

title: PAC Learnability in the Realizable Case
informal: Consider binary classification: instances come from a domain $\mathcal{X}$ with distribution $D$, and their labels are produced by an unknown target function $f:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}$. The true error of a classifier $h$ is $L_{D,f}(h)=D\{x: h(x)\ne f(x)\}$. The pair $(D,f)$ is realizable by the class $\mathcal{H}$ when some $h^\star\in\mathcal{H}$ has $L_{D,f}(h^\star)=0$. A learning rule $A$ PAC-learns $\mathcal{H}$ with sample complexity $m$ when for every realizable $(D,f)$, every $\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, and every $n\ge m(\varepsilon,\delta)$, the labelled sample $S=\bigl((x_1,f(x_1)),\dots,(x_n,f(x_n))\bigr)$ built from an independent sample $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of $D$ satisfies $$\Pr\bigl[L_{D,f}(A(S))\le\varepsilon\bigr]\;\ge\;1-\delta.$$
summary: A rule PAC-learns a class when, whenever some class member labels the data perfectly, enough samples make its output have error at most epsilon with probability at least 1 minus delta.
leanSignature:
def IsPACLearnerWith [MeasurableSpace X] (𝓗 : Set (X → Bool))
    (A : ∀ n : ℕ, Sample (X × Bool) n → (X → Bool)) (mSC : ℝ → ℝ → ℕ) :
    Prop :=
  ∀ (D : Measure X), IsProbabilityMeasure D → ∀ f : X → Bool,
    Realizable D f 𝓗 →
      ∀ ε δ : ℝ, 0 < ε → 0 < δ → δ < 1 →
        ∀ n : ℕ, mSC ε δ ≤ n →
          ENNReal.ofReal (1 - δ) ≤
            sampleLaw D n {s | errProb D f (A n (labeledBy f s)) ≤ ε}
formalizationNotes: Realizability is formalized as the existence of a class member whose disagreement set with the target is $D$-null, rather than as a zero integral, which is the same condition but stated without integrability side conditions. The learner receives a labelled sample obtained by applying the target to an unlabelled sample, so the randomness is carried by the instance sample alone. Labels are Booleans, and the classifier type is unrestricted; measurability of disagreement sets is a hypothesis where it is needed.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: The model is due to L. G. Valiant, “A theory of the learnable,” *Communications of the ACM* **27** (1984), 1134–1142; the name “probably approximately correct” and the systematic study of sample complexity in it are from A. Blumer, A. Ehrenfeucht, D. Haussler and M. K. Warmuth, “Learnability and the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension,” *Journal of the ACM* **36** (1989), 929–965.

title: Unbiasedness of the Empirical Risk
informal: Let $D$ be a distribution on the example domain, let $h$ be a fixed hypothesis whose loss is $D$-integrable, and let $n\ge 1$. If $S=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ is an independent sample from $D$, then $$\mathbb{E}_{S\sim D^{n}}\bigl[L_S(h)\bigr]\;=\;L_D(h).$$
summary: For a fixed hypothesis with integrable loss, the expected empirical risk over an independent sample equals the true risk.
leanSignature:
theorem integral_empRisk {ℓ : H → Z → ℝ} {h : H}
    (hint : Integrable (ℓ h) D)
    (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    ∫ s, empRisk ℓ s h ∂(sampleLaw D n) = risk D ℓ h
formalizationNotes: The sample law is the $n$-fold product measure, and the proof uses only that each coordinate projection pushes it forward to $D$; independence is not needed for the identity itself. The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ excludes the degenerate case in which the empirical risk is the junk value $0$ while the true risk need not be.

hypotheses.label: integrable loss
hypotheses.note: The loss of the fixed hypothesis is integrable against D, so its true risk is a genuine expectation.

hypotheses.label: nonempty sample
hypotheses.note: The sample size is at least one.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: That the training error of a fixed hypothesis is an unbiased estimate of its true error, and that this fails uniformly over a class, is the starting point of V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis, “On the uniform convergence of relative frequencies of events to their probabilities,” *Theory of Probability and Its Applications* **16** (1971), 264–280.

title: Empirical Risk Minimization on a Representative Sample
informal: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a hypothesis class, $\ell$ a loss, $D$ a distribution on the example domain, and $S$ a sample that is $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$-representative, meaning that $|L_S(g)-L_D(g)|\le\varepsilon/2$ for every $g\in\mathcal{H}$. If $h$ is an empirical risk minimizer over the class on that sample and the risks of the class are bounded below, then $$L_D(h)\;\le\;\inf_{g\in\mathcal{H}}L_D(g)+\varepsilon.$$
summary: On a sample that is epsilon-over-two-representative, any empirical risk minimizer has true risk within epsilon of the best in the class.
formalizationNotes: The bounded-below hypothesis is an artefact of stating the best-in-class risk as an infimum of a set of reals: without it the infimum is the junk value $0$ and the inequality would be false. It is discharged from nonnegativity of the loss in every application. The approximate-minimizer version is the companion theorem `risk_le_bestRisk_add_of_isApproxERM_of_uniformDeviation` in the same file.

hypotheses.label: representative sample
hypotheses.note: Every hypothesis in the class has empirical risk within ε/2 of its true risk on this sample.

hypotheses.label: empirical risk minimizer
hypotheses.note: The hypothesis lies in the class and no member of the class has smaller empirical risk on the sample.

hypotheses.label: risks bounded below
hypotheses.note: The set of true risks of members of the class is bounded below, so its infimum is genuine.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: The reduction of learnability to uniform convergence over the class is due to V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis, “On the uniform convergence of relative frequencies of events to their probabilities,” *Theory of Probability and Its Applications* **16** (1971), 264–280.

title: Uniform Convergence Implies Agnostic PAC Learnability
informal: Suppose the class $\mathcal{H}$ has the uniform convergence property with sample complexity $m^{\mathrm{UC}}$: for every distribution, accuracy $\varepsilon$ and confidence $\delta$, a sample of size at least $m^{\mathrm{UC}}(\varepsilon,\delta)$ is $\varepsilon$-representative with probability at least $1-\delta$. Let $A$ be a rule that returns an empirical risk minimizer over the class at every sample, and suppose the loss is nonnegative. Then $A$ agnostically PAC-learns $\mathcal{H}$ with sample complexity $$m(\varepsilon,\delta)\;=\;m^{\mathrm{UC}}\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\delta\right),$$ that is, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over a sample of that size, $L_D(A(S))\le\inf_{g\in\mathcal{H}}L_D(g)+\varepsilon$.
summary: A class with the uniform convergence property is agnostically PAC learnable by any empirical risk minimizer, with the sample complexity of uniform convergence at half the accuracy.
leanSignature:
theorem isAgnosticPACLearnerWith_of_hasUniformConvergenceWith
    {mUC : ℝ → ℝ → ℕ} {A : ∀ m : ℕ, Sample Z m → H}
    (hUC : HasUniformConvergenceWith 𝓗 ℓ mUC)
    (hA : ∀ (m : ℕ) (s : Sample Z m), IsERM 𝓗 ℓ s (A m s))
    (hpos : ∀ h z, 0 ≤ ℓ h z) :
    IsAgnosticPACLearnerWith 𝓗 ℓ A (fun ε δ => mUC (ε / 2) δ)
formalizationNotes: The empirical risk minimizer is supplied as data together with the hypothesis that it minimizes at every sample, rather than constructed: the book's $\mathrm{ERM}_{\mathcal{H}}$ is a choice function whose existence and measurability are not part of the statement. Nonnegativity of the loss is required on all hypotheses, not only those in the class, since it is used to bound the risk image below.

hypotheses.label: uniform convergence
hypotheses.note: For every distribution and every sample size at least m-UC(ε, δ), the sample is ε-representative with probability at least 1 − δ.

hypotheses.label: ERM selector
hypotheses.note: At every sample size and every sample, the rule returns a hypothesis in the class of minimal empirical risk.

hypotheses.label: nonnegative loss
hypotheses.note: The loss is nonnegative at every hypothesis and example.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: That uniform convergence over the class suffices for learning by empirical risk minimization is due to V. N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis, “On the uniform convergence of relative frequencies of events to their probabilities,” *Theory of Probability and Its Applications* **16** (1971), 264–280; the converse for binary classification is in A. Blumer, A. Ehrenfeucht, D. Haussler and M. K. Warmuth, “Learnability and the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension,” *Journal of the ACM* **36** (1989), 929–965.

title: Consistent Hypotheses in a Finite Class Generalize
informal: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite class of binary classifiers on $\mathcal{X}$, let $D$ be a distribution on $\mathcal{X}$ and $f$ a target labelling function, and write $L_{D,f}(h)=D\{x:h(x)\ne f(x)\}$ for the true error. Assume each disagreement set is measurable, $\varepsilon>0$, $\delta\in(0,1)$ and that the sample size satisfies $n\ge\log(|\mathcal{H}|/\delta)/\varepsilon$. Then for an independent sample $x_1,\dots,x_n$ from $D$, $$\Pr\Bigl[\,\exists\,h\in\mathcal{H}\ \text{with}\ h(x_i)=f(x_i)\ \text{for all } i\ \text{and}\ L_{D,f}(h)>\varepsilon\,\Bigr]\;\le\;\delta.$$
summary: For a finite class and enough samples, every hypothesis consistent with the data has true error at most epsilon, with probability at least 1 minus delta.
leanSignature:
theorem finiteClass_realizable_uniform (𝓗 : Finset (X → Bool)) {ε δ : ℝ}
    (hmeas : ∀ h ∈ 𝓗, MeasurableSet {x | h x ≠ f x})
    (hε : 0 < ε)
    (hδ : 0 < δ) (hδ1 : δ < 1)
    (hn : Real.log (𝓗.card / δ) / ε ≤ n) :
    sampleLaw D n
        {s | ∃ h ∈ 𝓗, (∀ i, h (s i) = f (s i)) ∧ ε < errProb D f h} ≤
      ENNReal.ofReal δ
formalizationNotes: The event is stated as the book's bad event, over consistent hypotheses in the class, rather than over the output of a particular learning rule; under realizability an empirical risk minimizer is consistent almost surely, and that step is carried out separately in the PAC corollary of the same file. The sample size hypothesis is the book's inequality without a ceiling. Each consistency event is a product cylinder, so its probability is exactly the $n$-th power of the agreement probability.

hypotheses.label: measurable disagreement
hypotheses.note: For each hypothesis in the class, the set of instances where it differs from the target is measurable.

hypotheses.label: positive accuracy
hypotheses.note: The accuracy parameter ε is positive.

hypotheses.label: confidence in (0,1)
hypotheses.note: The confidence parameter δ lies strictly between 0 and 1.

hypotheses.label: sample size
hypotheses.note: The sample size is at least log(|ℐ|/δ)/ε.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: The union-bound argument for finite classes in the realizable case is due to L. G. Valiant, “A theory of the learnable,” *Communications of the ACM* **27** (1984), 1134–1142, and was developed into the sample-complexity framework used here by A. Blumer, A. Ehrenfeucht, D. Haussler and M. K. Warmuth, “Learnability and the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension,” *Journal of the ACM* **36** (1989), 929–965.

title: Finite Classes Are PAC Learnable
informal: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite nonempty class of binary classifiers on $\mathcal{X}$ with measurable disagreement sets against every labelling function, and let $A$ be a rule that returns a classifier of minimal training error over the class. Then $A$ PAC-learns $\mathcal{H}$ with sample complexity $$m(\varepsilon,\delta)\;=\;\left\lceil\frac{\log(|\mathcal{H}|/\delta)}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil:$$ for every distribution $D$ on $\mathcal{X}$ and every target $f$ realized with zero error by some member of the class, and every sample size at least $m(\varepsilon,\delta)$, the output has true error at most $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$.
summary: Any empirical risk minimizer PAC-learns a finite class with sample complexity the ceiling of log of the class size over delta, divided by epsilon.
leanSignature:
theorem finiteClass_isPACLearnerWith (𝓗 : Finset (X → Bool))
    {A : ∀ m : ℕ, Sample (X × Bool) m → (X → Bool)}
    (h𝓗 : 𝓗.Nonempty)
    (hmeas : ∀ (g : X → Bool), ∀ h ∈ 𝓗, MeasurableSet {x | h x ≠ g x})
    (hA : ∀ (m : ℕ) (s : Sample (X × Bool) m),
      IsERM (↑𝓗 : Set (X → Bool)) zeroOneLoss s (A m s)) :
    IsPACLearnerWith (↑𝓗 : Set (X → Bool)) A
      (fun ε δ => ⌈Real.log (𝓗.card / δ) / ε⌉₊)
formalizationNotes: Realizability supplies a class member whose disagreement set with the target is null, hence whose empirical risk vanishes almost surely; the almost-sure qualifier that the book leaves implicit is carried explicitly through the event algebra, which is why every empirical risk minimizer, and not merely the consistent ones, is covered. Measurability of disagreement sets is required against every labelling function, since the target is universally quantified.

title: Finite Classes Have the Uniform Convergence Property
informal: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite nonempty hypothesis class and let $\ell$ be a loss with values in $[0,1]$ and measurable in the example for each hypothesis in the class. Then $\mathcal{H}$ has the uniform convergence property with sample complexity $$m^{\mathrm{UC}}(\varepsilon,\delta)\;=\;\left\lceil\frac{\log\bigl(2|\mathcal{H}|/\delta\bigr)}{2\varepsilon^{2}}\right\rceil,$$ that is, for every distribution $D$ and every sample size at least $m^{\mathrm{UC}}(\varepsilon,\delta)$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ the sample satisfies $|L_S(h)-L_D(h)|\le\varepsilon$ simultaneously for all $h\in\mathcal{H}$.
summary: A finite class with losses in the unit interval has the uniform convergence property with sample complexity logarithmic in the class size and quadratic in the inverse accuracy.
leanSignature:
theorem finiteClass_hasUniformConvergenceWith (𝓗 : Finset H)
    (h𝓗 : 𝓗.Nonempty)
    (hrange : ∀ h ∈ 𝓗, ∀ z, ℓ h z ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1)
    (hmeas : ∀ h ∈ 𝓗, Measurable (ℓ h)) :
    HasUniformConvergenceWith (↑𝓗 : Set H) ℓ
      (fun ε δ => ⌈Real.log (2 * 𝓗.card / δ) / (2 * ε ^ 2)⌉₊)
formalizationNotes: The per-hypothesis tail is assembled from the project's sub-Gaussian Hoeffding bound with variance proxy $1/4$ for a $[0,1]$-valued variable, applied to the coordinate stream of the product sample law and to its negation, which reproduces the book's constant $2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$ exactly. The class is a finite set, so its cardinality is the one appearing in the bound. The intermediate deviation bound $2|\mathcal{H}|e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}$ is available separately in the same file.

N. Vapnik and A. Ya. Chervonenkis (1971).

title: Finite Classes Are Agnostic PAC Learnable
informal: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite nonempty hypothesis class, let $\ell$ be a loss with values in $[0,1]$ on the class that is nonnegative everywhere, and let $A$ be a rule that returns a hypothesis of minimal empirical risk over the class; assume also that the loss of each class member is measurable in the example. Then $A$ agnostically PAC-learns $\mathcal{H}$ with sample complexity $$m(\varepsilon,\delta)\;=\;\left\lceil\frac{2\log\bigl(2|\mathcal{H}|/\delta\bigr)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right\rceil,$$ so that with probability at least $1-\delta$ over a sample of that size, $L_D(A(S))\le\inf_{g\in\mathcal{H}}L_D(g)+\varepsilon$ for every distribution $D$.
summary: Any empirical risk minimizer agnostically PAC-learns a finite class with sample complexity twice log of twice the class size over delta, divided by epsilon squared.
leanSignature:
theorem finiteClass_isAgnosticPACLearnerWith (𝓗 : Finset H)
    {A : ∀ m : ℕ, Sample Z m → H}
    (h𝓗 : 𝓗.Nonempty)
    (hrange : ∀ h ∈ 𝓗, ∀ z, ℓ h z ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1)
    (hmeas : ∀ h ∈ 𝓗, Measurable (ℓ h))
    (hA : ∀ (m : ℕ) (s : Sample Z m), IsERM (↑𝓗 : Set H) ℓ s (A m s))
    (hpos : ∀ h z, 0 ≤ ℓ h z) :
    IsAgnosticPACLearnerWith (↑𝓗 : Set H) ℓ A
      (fun ε δ => ⌈2 * Real.log (2 * 𝓗.card / δ) / ε ^ 2⌉₊)
formalizationNotes: The bound is the uniform convergence property of the same class at accuracy $\varepsilon/2$, fed through the general implication from uniform convergence to agnostic PAC learnability; the only arithmetic is the identity relating the two ceilings, which is stated so that it also holds at the degenerate value $\varepsilon = 0$. Nonnegativity is required at every hypothesis, including those outside the class, because it supplies the lower bound on the risk image that makes the best-in-class infimum genuine.

title: Rademacher Complexity
informal: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a set of vectors and let $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ be independent signs, each equal to $+1$ or $-1$ with probability $\tfrac12$. The Rademacher complexity of $A$ is $$R(A)\;=\;\frac1n\,\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\Bigl[\,\sup_{a\in A}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i a_i\Bigr].$$
summary: The Rademacher complexity of a set of vectors is the expected supremum of its correlation with a uniformly random sign vector, normalized by the dimension.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def radComplexity (A : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) : ℝ :=
  (n : ℝ)⁻¹ * signAvg n (fun ε => sSup ((fun a => ∑ i, ε i * a i) '' A))
formalizationNotes: The sign expectation is a finite average over the $2^n$ Boolean patterns, not an integral, so the definition needs no measure theory; the bridge to the product measure of independent signs is a separate lemma. The supremum is the supremum of the image set rather than an indexed supremum over the set, which avoids the junk floor at $0$ that the latter carries in Lean; the degenerate values are $R(\varnothing) = 0$, $R = 0$ for an image unbounded above, and $R = 0$ at $n = 0$, so theorems carry nonemptiness and (usually) finiteness hypotheses.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: Rademacher averages as a complexity measure for learning were introduced by V. Koltchinskii, “Rademacher penalties and structural risk minimization,” *IEEE Transactions on Information Theory* **47** (2001), 1902–1914, and by P. L. Bartlett and S. Mendelson, “Rademacher and Gaussian complexities: risk bounds and structural results,” *Journal of Machine Learning Research* **3** (2002), 463–482; the underlying symmetrization technique is classical in empirical process theory, see M. Ledoux and M. Talagrand, *Probability in Banach Spaces*, Springer, 1991.

title: Empirical Rademacher Complexity
informal: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of real-valued functions on the example domain, indexed by a set $K$, and let $S=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ be a sample. Evaluating the family on the sample produces the set of vectors $$\mathcal{F}\circ S\;=\;\bigl\{\,(f(z_1),\dots,f(z_n))\;:\;f\in\mathcal{F}\,\bigr\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n},$$ and the empirical Rademacher complexity of $\mathcal{F}$ on $S$ is the Rademacher complexity of that set, $$R(\mathcal{F}\circ S)\;=\;\frac1n\,\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\Bigl[\,\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_i f(z_i)\Bigr].$$
summary: The empirical Rademacher complexity of a function family on a sample is the Rademacher complexity of the set of its evaluation vectors on that sample.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def empRad (F : ι → Z → ℝ) (K : Set ι) (s : Sample Z n) : ℝ :=
  radComplexity (evalFamily F K s)
formalizationNotes: The family is given as a function on an index type together with a subset of indices, rather than as a set of functions, so that a hypothesis class and its loss family can be indexed by the same set. The evaluation set is the image of the index set, so the same degenerate conventions as for the Rademacher complexity apply.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: Data-dependent complexity measures of this form, and their use as penalties in structural risk minimization, are due to V. Koltchinskii, “Rademacher penalties and structural risk minimization,” *IEEE Transactions on Information Theory* **47** (2001), 1902–1914, and P. L. Bartlett and S. Mendelson, “Rademacher and Gaussian complexities: risk bounds and structural results,” *Journal of Machine Learning Research* **3** (2002), 463–482.

title: Symmetrization
informal: Let $\mathcal{F}=\{F_k\}_{k\in K}$ be a family of real-valued functions on the example domain, measurable in the example, with $K$ nonempty and countable, and suppose the family is uniformly bounded, $|F_k(z)|\le c$ for all $k\in K$ and all $z$. Then for every distribution $D$ and every sample size $n\ge1$, $$\mathbb{E}_{S\sim D^{n}}\Bigl[\,\sup_{k\in K}\bigl(L_D(F_k)-L_S(F_k)\bigr)\Bigr]\;\le\;2\,\mathbb{E}_{S\sim D^{n}}\bigl[R(\mathcal{F}\circ S)\bigr].$$
summary: The expected supremum of the gap between true and empirical risk over a bounded family is at most twice the expected Rademacher complexity of the family on the sample.
leanSignature:
theorem integral_sup_risk_sub_empRisk_le_two_mul_integral_empRad
    (F : ι → Z → ℝ) (K : Set ι) {c : ℝ}
    (hKc : K.Countable)
    (hK : K.Nonempty)
    (hmeas : ∀ k, Measurable (F k))
    (hbdd : ∀ k ∈ K, ∀ z, |F k z| ≤ c)
    (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    ∫ s, sSup ((fun k => risk D F k - empRisk F s k) '' K)
        ∂(sampleLaw D n) ≤
      2 * ∫ s, empRad F K s ∂(sampleLaw D n)
formalizationNotes: This is the one-sided form, without absolute values, which is what the constants of the high-probability Rademacher bounds require; the project's general symmetrization lemma proves the absolute-value form, so this version is proved afresh by the book's argument. Countability of the index set and the uniform bound are standing conventions for suprema in this development: they make the supremum measurable and integrable without a separability discussion. Suprema are taken over the image set, so no indexed-supremum junk value can intervene.

title: Massart's Lemma
informal: Let $A=\{a_1,\dots,a_N\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a finite nonempty set of vectors with mean $\bar a=\tfrac1N\sum_{j}a_j$. Then $$R(A)\;\le\;\max_{a\in A}\lVert a-\bar a\rVert_2\;\frac{\sqrt{2\log N}}{n},$$ where $R(A)$ is the Rademacher complexity of $A$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm.
summary: The Rademacher complexity of a finite set of vectors is at most its radius about the mean times the square root of twice the log-cardinality, divided by the dimension.
leanSignature:
theorem massart (A : Finset (Fin n → ℝ))
    (hne : A.Nonempty) :
    radComplexity (↑A : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) ≤
      (A.sup' hne fun a =>
          Real.sqrt (∑ i, (a i - (A.card : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ b ∈ A, b i) ^ 2)) *
        Real.sqrt (2 * Real.log A.card) / n
formalizationNotes: The Euclidean norm is written out as the square root of a sum of squares, because the ambient norm on the space of coordinate functions is the supremum norm. The class is a finite set so that the maximum is attained and the supremum in the Rademacher complexity is genuine. The centred variant, in which the mean is replaced by an arbitrary centre and the maximum by a radius bound, is proved alongside and is the form used downstream.

hypotheses.label: nonempty finite set
hypotheses.note: The set of vectors is finite and nonempty.

reference.formal: S. Shalev-Shwartz and S. Ben-David, *Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms*, Cambridge University Press, 2014.
reference.biblio: The bound is due to P. Massart, “Some applications of concentration inequalities to statistics,” *Annales de la Faculté des Sciences de Toulouse* **9** (2000), 245–303; the underlying sub-Gaussian maximal inequality is classical, see W. Hoeffding, “Probability inequalities for sums of bounded random variables,” *Journal of the American Statistical Association* **58** (1963), 13–30.

title: Contraction Lemma for Rademacher Complexity
informal: Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be finite and nonempty and let $\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be $\rho$-Lipschitz, so that $|\varphi_i(x)-\varphi_i(y)|\le\rho|x-y|$ for all $x,y$, with $\rho\ge0$. Write $\varphi\circ A=\{(\varphi_1(a_1),\dots,\varphi_n(a_n)):a\in A\}$. Then $$R(\varphi\circ A)\;\le\;\rho\,R(A).$$
summary: Composing each coordinate with a rho-Lipschitz map multiplies the Rademacher complexity of a finite set by at most rho.
leanSignature:
theorem radComplexity_contraction (A : Finset (Fin n → ℝ))
    (φ : Fin n → ℝ → ℝ) {ρ : ℝ}
    (hne : A.Nonempty)
    (hρ : 0 ≤ ρ)
    (hφ : ∀ i a b, |φ i a - φ i b| ≤ ρ * |a - b|) :
    radComplexity
        (↑(A.image fun a => fun i => φ i (a i)) : Set (Fin n → ℝ)) ≤
      ρ * radComplexity (↑A : Set (Fin n → ℝ))
formalizationNotes: This is the contraction of a Lipschitz composition inside a supremum, distinct from the coefficient contraction principle for norms of sign-weighted sums that appears elsewhere in the project. The maps may differ from coordinate to coordinate, as in the book. The class is a finite set so that suprema are attained, which the coordinate-by-coordinate pairing argument needs. The book's displayed inequality contains a typographical slip in one subscript; the statement here follows the corrected reading.

title: Rademacher Generalization Bound
informal: Let $\mathcal{F}=\{F_k\}_{k\in K}$ be a family of loss functions on the example domain, indexed by a countable nonempty set and measurable in the example, with $|F_k(z)|\le c$ for all $k\in K$ and all $z$. Let $n\ge1$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$. Then with probability at least $1-\delta$ over a sample $S$ of size $n$ drawn independently from $D$, simultaneously for every $k\in K$, $$L_D(F_k)-L_S(F_k)\;\le\;2\,\mathbb{E}_{S'\sim D^{n}}\bigl[R(\mathcal{F}\circ S')\bigr]\;+\;c\,\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(2/\delta)}{n}}.$$
summary: With high probability, every member of a uniformly bounded family has true risk exceeding its empirical risk by at most twice the expected Rademacher complexity plus a square-root deviation term.
leanSignature:
theorem rademacher_generalization_expected {δ : ℝ}
    (hKc : K.Countable)
    (hK : K.Nonempty)
    (hmeas : ∀ k, Measurable (F k))
    (hbdd : ∀ k ∈ K, ∀ z, |F k z| ≤ c)
    (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (hδ : 0 < δ) (hδ1 : δ < 1) :
    ENNReal.ofReal (1 - δ) ≤
      sampleLaw D n {s | ∀ k ∈ K,
        risk D F k - empRisk F s k ≤
          2 * (∫ s', empRad F K s' ∂(sampleLaw D n)) +
            c * Real.sqrt (2 * Real.log (2 / δ) / n)}
formalizationNotes: The bounded-differences inequality is taken from the project's McDiarmid development, which is where the standard Borel and nonemptiness instances on the example space come from; they are formalization conventions with no counterpart in the book. The index set is countable and the family uniformly bounded, so that the supremum over the class is measurable and integrable. The degenerate case $c = 0$, in which every loss vanishes and both sides are $0$, is treated separately because the tail calibration divides by $c^2$.

informal: Let $\mathcal{F}=\{F_k\}_{k\in K}$ be a family of loss functions indexed by a countable nonempty set, measurable in the example and bounded by $c$ in absolute value. title: Excess Risk of Empirical Risk Minimization via Rademacher Complexity
informal: Let $\mathcal{F}=\{F_k\}_{k\in K}$ be a family of loss functions indexed by a countable nonempty set, measurable in the example and bounded by $c$ in absolute value. Let $A$ be a rule that returns an index in $K$ minimizing the empirical risk over the family at each sample, and let $k^\star$ be any fixed competitor in $K$. For $n\ge1$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over a sample $S$ of size $n$ from $D$, $$L_D\bigl(F_{A(S)}\bigr)-L_D\bigl(F_{k^\star}\bigr)\;\le\;2\,R(\mathcal{F}\circ S)\;+\;5c\,\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(8/\delta)}{n}}.$$
summary: With high probability the excess risk of an empirical risk minimizer over any fixed competitor is at most twice the empirical Rademacher complexity plus a square-root deviation term.
leanSignature:
theorem rademacher_erm_excess {A : Sample Z n → ι} {kStar : ι} {δ : ℝ}
    (hKc : K.Countable)
    (hK : K.Nonempty)
    (hmeas : ∀ k, Measurable (F k))
    (hbdd : ∀ k ∈ K, ∀ z, |F k z| ≤ c)
    (hA : ∀ s, A s ∈ K ∧ ∀ k ∈ K, empRisk F s (A s) ≤ empRisk F s k)
    (hkStar : kStar ∈ K)
    (hn : 1 ≤ n)
    (hδ : 0 < δ) (hδ1 : δ < 1) :
    ENNReal.ofReal (1 - δ) ≤
      sampleLaw D n {s |
        risk D F (A s) - risk D F kStar ≤
          2 * empRad F K s + 5 * c * Real.sqrt (2 * Real.log (8 / δ) / n)}
formalizationNotes: Three deviations are combined by a union bound at confidence $\delta/8$ each: the worst-case gap, the empirical Rademacher complexity, and the empirical risk of the fixed competitor. The last of these is obtained from the same bounded-differences brick applied to the competitor's empirical risk, whose mean is its true risk and whose bounded-differences constant is again $2c/n$, rather than from a separate Hoeffding bound; the total lands inside the book's frozen constant $5c$. The case $c = 0$ is treated separately.

title: Polynomial Growth of the Loss Patterns of a VC Class
informal: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a class of binary classifiers on $\mathcal{X}$, identified with the class of sets $\{x:h(x)=1\}$, and suppose its VC dimension is at most $d$ — no set of more than $d$ instances is shattered, i.e. has every one of its labellings realized by a member of the class (see VC dimension). Fix a labelled sample $S=\bigl((x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)\bigr)$ and consider the set of loss patterns $$\bigl\{\,(\mathbf 1[h(x_1)\ne y_1],\dots,\mathbf 1[h(x_n)\ne y_n])\;:\;h\in\mathcal{H}\,\bigr\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}.$$ If $d\ge1$ and $n>d+1$, the number of distinct loss patterns is at most $$\Bigl(\frac{en}{d}\Bigr)^{d},$$ and in general at most $\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom{n}{j}$.

title: Finite VC Dimension Implies Agnostic PAC Learnability
informal: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a nonempty countable class of binary classifiers on $\mathcal{X}$ whose VC dimension is at most $d$, with $d\ge1$ and measurable error sets. title: On-Average-Replace-One Stability
informal: Let $A$ be a learning rule and $\ell$ a loss. Given a sample $S=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$, an index $i$ and a fresh example $z'$, write $S^{(i)}$ for the sample obtained from $S$ by replacing its $i$-th example by $z'$. The rule is on-average-replace-one stable with rate $\epsilon(n)$ when, for every distribution $D$ on the example domain, $$\mathbb{E}_{S\sim D^{n},\,z'\sim D}\;\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl[\ell\bigl(A(S^{(i)}),z_i\bigr)-\ell\bigl(A(S),z_i\bigr)\Bigr]\;\le\;\epsilon(n).$$
summary: A rule is on-average-replace-one stable with a given rate when the expected increase in loss caused by replacing one training example is bounded by that rate.
leanSignature:
def OnAvgReplaceOneStableWith [MeasurableSpace Z] (ℓ : H → Z → ℝ)
    (A : ∀ m : ℕ, Sample Z m → H) (rate : ℕ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (D : Measure Z), IsProbabilityMeasure D →
    ∀ m : ℕ, stabilityGap D ℓ (A m) ≤ rate m
formalizationNotes: Stability is defined on average, which is the book's only formal notion; the pointwise bound that the Lipschitz analysis of regularized loss minimization actually establishes is strictly stronger and is relaxed to this notion where it is used. The joint law of the sample and the fresh example is the product of the sample law with the distribution, and the average over indices is an explicit sum rather than an expectation over a uniform index variable. The rate is a function of the sample size, with one hypothesis class for each size.

title: Stable Rules Do Not Overfit
informal: Let $A$ be a learning rule, $\ell$ a loss, and $D$ a distribution on the example domain, and let the sample size be at least one. Writing $S^{(i)}$ for the sample $S$ with its $i$-th example replaced by an independent fresh example $z'$, and assuming the losses involved are integrable, $$\mathbb{E}_{S\sim D^{n}}\Bigl[L_D\bigl(A(S)\bigr)-L_S\bigl(A(S)\bigr)\Bigr]\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{S\sim D^{n},\,z'\sim D}\;\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigl[\ell\bigl(A(S^{(i)}),z_i\bigr)-\ell\bigl(A(S),z_i\bigr)\Bigr].$$

title: Tikhonov Regularization Is a Stabilizer
informal: Let $W$ be a real inner-product space, and consider regularized loss minimization: on a sample $S$ of size $n$ the rule returns a global minimizer $A(S)$ of $L_S(w)+\lambda\lVert w\rVert^{2}$, with $\lambda>0$. title: Change of Measure (Donsker–Varadhan)
informal: Let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on a countable index set with $Q$ absolutely continuous with respect to $P$ and finite Kullback–Leibler divergence $\mathrm{KL}(Q\Vert P)$, and let $f$ be a functional on the index set with $Q$-integrable value and $P$-integrable exponential. Then $$\mathbb{E}_{k\sim Q}\bigl[f(k)\bigr]\;\le\;\mathrm{KL}(Q\Vert P)\;+\;\log\,\mathbb{E}_{k\sim P}\bigl[e^{f(k)}\bigr].$$
summary: For a posterior absolutely continuous with respect to a prior, the posterior mean of a functional is at most the Kullback-Leibler divergence plus the log of the prior's exponential moment.

The two integrability hypotheses are supplied by boundedness of the loss in the PAC-Bayes application. The index set is countable with the discrete structure, which is the scope of this development, although the proof itself goes through the tilted-measure machinery and does not use discreteness.

title: PAC-Bayes Generalization Bound
informal: Consider randomized predictors: a countable family of hypotheses $\{F_k\}_{k}$ with losses taking values in $[0,1]$ and measurable in the example, a prior distribution $P$ over the index chosen before seeing the data, and a posterior $Q$ that may depend on the sample. Write $L_D(Q)=\mathbb{E}_{k\sim Q}[L_D(F_k)]$ and $L_S(Q)=\mathbb{E}_{k\sim Q}[L_S(F_k)]$ for the Gibbs true and empirical risks. Let $n\ge2$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$. Then with probability at least $1-\delta$ over a sample $S$ of size $n$ drawn independently from $D$, simultaneously for every posterior $Q$ absolutely continuous with respect to $P$ and of finite divergence, $$L_D(Q)\;\le\;L_S(Q)\;+\;\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{KL}(Q\Vert P)+\ln\bigl(2n/\delta\bigr)}{2(n-1)}}.$$
